items.title: Sokoto attack : Beggar’s son shot by terrorist needs N190,000 for scan
items.summary: By Evelyn Usman One of the five persons who sustained bullet wounds during last week’s attack on Girkau community in Kebbe Local Government Area of Sokoto State by suspected bandits is lying helpless at the Usman Danfodiyo University Teaching Hospital (UDUTH), unable to afford the N190,000 required for aMagnetic Resonance Imaging ,MRI and Computed Tomography […] The post Sokoto attack : Beggar’s s
items.body: By Evelyn Usman One of the five persons who sustained bullet wounds during last week’s attack on Girkau community in Kebbe Local Government Area of Sokoto State by suspected bandits is lying helpless at the Usman Danfodiyo University Teaching Hospital (UDUTH), unable to afford the N190,000 required for a Magnetic Resonance Imaging ,MRI and Computed Tomography CT scan , prescribed by doctors. The victim, 30-year-old Jamilu Abubakar, was shot in the back by suspected bandits while returning from his farmland, where he had gone to harvest millet. Abubakar, who spoke in an inaudible tone with the aid of an interpreter from his hospital bed, said he had lost sensation from his chest down to his lower limbs since he was shot. His hope of raising the required amount is dim, as he revealed that his father is physically challenged and begs to feed his family. According to him, “I cannot feel anything from my chest down to my lower limbs. Even if they pierced me with a sharp object, I cannot feel it. Doctors attending to me have requested a CT scan and MRI to determine the extent of the injury, but my family is unable to raise the amount required for the test. The Radiographer said it will cost N190,000, but we don’t have the money.” Recounting how he was shot, Abubakar said he was returning from his farmland after harvesting millet when he sighted the armed men and attempted to flee. “When I saw the armed men, I tried to run, but they shot me in the back. I was on the floor until they left. My father and other people who came out of hiding managed to rush me to the hospital. I have been given drips, but further treatment will depend on the outcome of the CT scan. “My father is crippled. He begs to eat and uses the money he gets from begging to feed his children. Now, we don’t have money for my treatment,” he stated, appealing to well-meaning Nigerians to come to his aid. Meanwhile, five persons have now been confirmed dead in the attack. Those killed were identified as Abubakar Zagu, popularly known as Dogon Attah; Abubakar Aliyu; Babangida Chali; and Adamu Dan Gashuwa Dukura. The other injured victims were identified as Dahru Dantunba, Jamilu Madugu, Sani Danbuga, the community secretary, and Basiru Dansalah. Meanwhile, the latest military operation has brought renewed hope to residents of some communities in Kebbe Local Government Area who had been living in fear after receiving threat letters from bandits. Residents said the presence of troops and their incursion into the forests, where weapons, ammunition and motorcycles were recovered, had boosted their confidence and reassured them that the terrorists could be pushed back. However, they appealed to the military not to withdraw from the area immediately, stressing that a sustained presence was necessary to prevent the criminals from regrouping and returning to the communities. The post Sokoto attack : Beggar’s son shot by terrorist needs N190,000 for scan appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: The Silent Return: How Diphtheria Killed 39 Children in Zamfara and UNICEF, Health Ministry’s Dash for Urgent Vaccination
items.summary: Onuminya Innocent The ward at the Infectious Disease Centre in Damba is quiet in a way that feels wrong. Fluorescent lights hum above rows of iron beds. Mothers sit on
items.body: Onuminya Innocent The ward at the Infectious Disease Centre in Damba is quiet in a way that feels wrong. Fluorescent lights hum above rows of iron beds. Mothers sit on plastic chairs, cloths pressed to fevered foreheads. Nurses move fast between patients, but their voices are low. Last week, the Zamfara State Ministry of Health confirmed what many families here already feared: an outbreak of diphtheria has claimed 39 lives. The ministry also recorded another 261 suspected cases across 10 local government areas. Most of the faces in these beds are small. Health workers say many of the children are between six and ten months old. “Some of them came in too late,” a nurse at the WCWC Primary Healthcare Centre in Kwata, Gusau, said as she checked a child’s throat with a torchlight, adding, “By the time the parents realise it’s not just a cough, the breathing is already difficult.” Diphtheria, caused by Corynebacterium, attacks the nose, throat, and sometimes the skin. The early signs look ordinary: fever, runny nose, sore throat, cough, red eyes. Then comes the neck swelling. Then the struggle to breathe. Without antitoxins and antibiotics, it kills. What is new is how quickly it has moved this year. A disease of missed chances The numbers paint a worrying picture. Gusau Local Government Area alone accounts for 191 of the 261 suspected cases—the highest in the state. Laboratory tests have confirmed some cases, while surveillance teams continue to test and trace contacts across communities. The state government responded immediately. The Ministry of Health convened a rapid response team and deployed it to affected areas to identify new cases, provide emergency treatment, and prevent further spread. Rilwan Musa, Permanent Secretary of the Zamfara State Ministry of Health, said that the response has full backing from Governor Dauda Lawal’s administration and development partners. “We mobilised across the state the moment we saw the trend,” Musa told THISDAY. “But we need government at all levels to intensify efforts – more vaccines, more health workers, more sensitisation in every ward. This cannot be a one-state fight.” But behind the mobilisation is a harder truth: most of the children who died had not been vaccinated. National data backs that up. According to UNICEF, only 22 per cent of confirmed diphtheria cases in Nigeria had received routine childhood immunisations. The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) reports that 68 per cent of confirmed cases nationwide involved unvaccinated people. “It’s heartbreaking to note that only 22 per cent of the confirmed cases received their routine childhood immunisation vaccinations,” said Cristian Munduate, UNICEF Representative in Nigeria. “Many children did not receive their vaccines during the COVID-19 lockdown. We now urgently need to catch up. These zero-dose children, those who haven’t received a single dose of vaccine, are a primary concern.” In Zamfara, that gap is visible. At Kwata PHC, health workers point to immunisation hesitancy and missed doses as major drivers of the spread. “We are begging parents,” the nurse added. “Please bring your wards for vaccination. The vaccines are free at all PHCs. Waiting costs lives. If your child misses a dose, go to the clinic today. Don’t wait for symptoms.” Ten LGAs, one fear The outbreak is not confined to Gusau. Cases have been reported in nine other LGAs, stretching response teams thin. From Kwata PHC, the rapid response team proceeded to Damba to check on patients receiving care at the Infectious Disease Centre. Some were on oxygen. Some were stable. All were children. Diphtheria thrives where routine vaccination drops. Nationwide, the outbreak has hit Kano, Yobe, Katsina, Lagos, FCT, Sokoto, and Zamfara hardest—those seven states account for 98 per cent of suspected cases. Children aged 2 to 14 make up about 71.5 per cent of confirmed cases. The case fatality rate sits at 8.7 per cent. For every 100 children infected, nearly nine do not make it. In the last three years, NCDC says diphtheria has claimed over 1,300 lives across Nigeria. What happens next: A two-pronged responsibility In Damba, the immediate work is clinical: identify, isolate, treat. Antitoxin and antibiotics are being administered. Contacts are being traced. Health education teams are moving through markets and schools with megaphones and pamphlets. But health officials insist that treatment alone will not end this. For government, the demand is clear: intensify efforts. That means deploying more vaccines to rural PHCs, funding mobile vaccination teams, paying community health workers promptly, and sustaining surveillance even after the outbreak slows. For parents and caregivers, the responsibility is just as urgent: avail your wards for vaccination. The diphtheria vaccine is part of Nigeria’s routine immunisation and is provided free at primary healthcare centres. Children are to receive doses at six, 10, and 14 weeks, with boosters later. Catch-up campaigns are now being prioritised in Zamfara to reach “zero-dose” children. Health officials are asking communities to do three things: bring any child with fever, sore throat, or breathing difficulty to a clinic immediately; complete the full vaccination schedule; and report suspected cases early. At Kwata, a mother rocked her eight-month-old and whispered prayers. She had missed the second vaccine dose during the pandemic. “I thought we could wait,” she said. “I didn’t know it would come like this. I will take my other children tomorrow.” The weight of 39 Thirty-nine funerals in a matter of weeks. Thirty-nine names that will be read at community meetings. Thirty-nine empty spaces at dinner tables across 10 LGAs. The rapid response team will keep working. The vaccines are available. The message from the health ministry and UNICEF is simple and urgent: this disease is preventable—but only if government intensifies efforts and parents step forward. For now, Zamfara is in a race between the bacteria moving through unprotected children and the health workers trying to reach them first. In Damba ward, a nurse adjusts an IV and checks a chart. Outside, another ambulance pulls in. The fight is not over.

items.title: Spotlight on Nigerian Army’s Operational Gains in Rescue, Counter-terrorism
items.summary: The Nigerian Army has recorded significant operational successes from July to the first week of September, with troops involved in rescue operations, arrests, patrols, ambushes and weapons recovery across multiple
items.body: The Nigerian Army has recorded significant operational successes from July to the first week of September, with troops involved in rescue operations, arrests, patrols, ambushes and weapons recovery across multiple theatres. The period includes the rescue of 11 kidnapped persons and arrest of 21 suspects in July; 308 people rescued in a joint operation around Kainji Lake National Park; 21 abducted persons rescued in Kogi on August 31; and 25 more victims rescued in Katsina and Zamfara. Troops also recovered an RPG launcher, an AK-47 rifle, ammunition and 793 rounds of ammunition intercepted in Kaduna, as operations against terrorism, banditry and kidnapping continued nationwide. Chiemelie Ezeobi writes that this is in tandem with the Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu’s P.R.O.S.E operational framework Since taking over as Chief of Army Staff in October 2025, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu has made operational readiness, professionalism, innovation and joint operations central to his command philosophy. Months down the line, these key derivatives on intelligence, surveillance, target acquisition and reconnaissance, as well as cooperation with other security agencies, has played central figures in responding to Nigeria’s changing security environment. Which is why the operations carried out by the Nigerian Army, recorded specifically from July into the first week of September provide an early indication of how those priorities are being translated into activities by formations and units in the field. Taken in a wider context, the NA, alongside other security agencies, conducted 7,062 operations nationwide in July and August, neutralised 1,487 terrorists and insurgents, arrested 354 suspects and rescued 777 kidnapped victims. Rescue Operations Across Theatres Across different theatres of operations, the NA troops carried out rescues with the most notable being the rescue of 21 abducted persons in Kogi State on August 31, including 15 National Youth Service Corps members who were abducted while travelling from Abuja to Bayelsa State. The victims were rescued from the Egume and Ochaja forest areas of Dekina Local Government Area after troops of the Nigerian Army’s 12 Brigade joined other security agencies, hunters and vigilante groups in a search operation. In all, 21 victims, comprising eight males and 13 females, were rescued. The Kogi operation was one of several rescue and security operations conducted by the Army and other security actors during the period. Between July 21 and 22, operations under Operation HADIN KAI, Operation FANSAN YAMMA and Operation MESA led to the rescue of 11 kidnapped persons and the arrest of 21 suspected terrorists, collaborators, logistics suppliers and drug peddlers. Troops also discovered and destroyed improvised explosive devices during the operations, which covered Borno, Zamfara and Kogi states. By August, the scale of some rescue operations had increased as a joint security operation in the Kainji Lake National Park area resulted in the rescue of 308 people. The operation involved multiple security actors and therefore cannot be attributed to the Nigerian Army alone. The victims included 163 people abducted from Woro community in Kwara State and 145 others from Niger State. The operation highlighted the scale of kidnapping around forest and rural corridors linking parts of Kwara and Niger states, where security forces have had to conduct patrols over long distances and respond to intelligence on kidnapping gangs and other armed groups. Notably, Kogi provided another test of rapid response as on September 2, two women were reportedly abducted from a farm in Ajodomodo Village in Dekina Local Government Area. Troops of the 21 Battalion Quick Reaction Force responded to a distress call and pursued the kidnappers towards Agbodakodo Forest. The pursuit forced the abductors to abandon the victims. The women—a 15-year-old girl and a 30-year-old woman—were subsequently rescued and taken to the 21 Battalion Medical Reception Station for medical attention. The two incidents within days of each other placed the response capabilities of troops in the area under pressure, with 12 Brigade and other Army units under 2 Division continuing to form part of the security response to kidnapping and other threats affecting Kogi and adjoining states. Sustained Operations In The North-West. The same operational priorities have been reflected in the North-West, where troops have continued operations against terrorists and bandits across Kaduna, Katsina and Zamfara states. On September 4, troops of Operation FANSAN YAMMA rescued 25 kidnapped persons during separate operations in Katsina and Zamfara. Two victims were rescued during a night patrol along the Kwanar Kura axis of Sabuwa Local Government Area in Katsina State after troops engaged fleeing terrorists. In Zamfara, troops of Sector 2 rescued 23 civilians—three males and 20 females—during a fighting patrol on the outskirts of Wuya town in Anka Local Government Area. Preliminary information indicated that the victims had been abducted from Gummi Local Government Area and had spent about three weeks in captivity. They were evacuated for medical attention and further debriefing. The operations reflect the continued use of patrols, fighting patrols, engagements and intelligence-based responses against armed groups operating in the region. Weapons Recovery and Disruption The Nigerian Army’s recent operations have also focused on the weapons and logistics supporting terrorist and bandit activities. During an ambush along the Kwanar Jolof axis of Shinkafi-Zurmi in Zamfara, troops engaged terrorists and recovered an RPG launcher, an AK-47 rifle, magazines and ammunition. In another operation in Kaduna State, troops intercepted a vehicle carrying 793 rounds of ammunition concealed in a sack of grain. The operation was aimed at disrupting the movement of weapons to criminal elements. Other recent operations in the North-West also resulted in the recovery of weapons, ammunition and motorcycles from terrorists. The seizures form part of efforts to restrict the movement of arms and ammunition to armed groups operating across the region. The Wider Picture Army formations remain engaged in several major security theatres. In the North-East, troops continue counter-insurgency operations against Boko Haram and ISWAP. In the North-West and North-Central, formations are conducting operations against banditry and kidnapping, while other Army units remain involved in security operations in the South-East and other parts of the country. P.R.O.S.E and the Field Results The pattern of operations from July into the first week of September provides a basis for examining the application of the COAS’ strategic framework. From the rescue of 21 people in Kogi on August 31, to the recovery of an RPG launcher, AK-47 rifle and ammunition in Zamfara, the interception of 793 rounds of ammunition in Kaduna, and the rescue of 25 kidnapped persons in Katsina and Zamfara on September 4, the operations have continued into the first week of September. In the North-West, Operation FANSAN YAMMA has combined patrols, ambushes, fighting patrols, intelligence-led operations and weapons recovery against terrorist and bandit groups. Essentially, these activities correspond with key elements of Lieutenant General Shaibu’s P.R.O.S.E framework- Professional Excellence, Operational Readiness and Strategic Cooperation and Exemplary Leadership. Taken together, the activities provide an early operational record against which the priorities set out in Shaibu’s command philosophy can be assessed, with troops continuing to conduct rescue operations, patrols, arrests, engagements and weapons recovery across multiple theatres.

items.title: AVM Suleh Charges NAF Personnel to Embrace Sportsmanship as Vital Ingredient of National Security
items.summary: Chiemelie Ezeobi The Air Officer Commanding (AOC), Logistics Command, Air Vice Marshal Abubakar Suleh, has urged Nigerian Air Force personnel to embrace sportsmanship as part of their professional responsibility, describing
items.body: Chiemelie Ezeobi The Air Officer Commanding (AOC), Logistics Command, Air Vice Marshal Abubakar Suleh, has urged Nigerian Air Force personnel to embrace sportsmanship as part of their professional responsibility, describing it as a vital ingredient for strengthening the nation’s security architecture. Air Vice Marshal Suleh made the call in Lagos at the closing ceremony of the 2026 Third Quarter Headquarters Intra-Command Sports Competition, organised for personnel of Logistics Command and co-located units in the Lagos area. Air Vice Marshal Suleh said the competition showcased teamwork, endurance and tactical excellence across football, volleyball, basketball and handball, reflecting the qualities required of a combat-ready force. According to him, the quarterly sporting event is more than a contest for medals and trophies; it is a true test of resilience, discipline and unity. He noted that the initiative aligns with the Chief of the Air Staff’s command philosophy of promoting physical fitness, mental alertness and high morale among personnel. Air Vice Marshal Suleh added that a capable fighting force is built not only in classrooms and operational theatres but also on the sports field, where esprit de corps is developed and strengthened. The AOC congratulated all participating teams and athletes for their discipline, fair play and determination, while the captain of the winning Logistics football team, Sergeant Idoko Emmanuel, thanked God for the team’s victory. Senior officers from various arms of the Nigerian Armed Forces attended the event. The week-long competition was held across three venues — the NAFOM Gym, AMAO Court and ATO Field — and featured four competing groups: Group A, comprising HQ Logistics Command, 641 Communications, AFSS Ikeja and 613 FPG; Group B, made up of 643 ESD, 661 NAFH, 081 PAG/DOP and AETSC; Group C, comprising 651 BSG, 057 PIG, 051 PMG and 015 SIG; and Group D, comprising 631 ACMD, NADC, 304 HAG and 355 RW. At the close of the tournament, organisers released an official medal table showing results across all four disciplines. In basketball, Group D won Gold, Group B took Silver, and Group A settled for Bronze. In volleyball, Group D again claimed Gold, with Group B taking Silver and Group A Bronze. In handball, Group B won Gold, Group A took Silver, and Group D settled for Bronze. In football, Group A emerged Gold medallists, Group B took Silver, and Group C claimed Bronze. Tallying medals across all four sports, Group D finished with 2 Gold and 1 Bronze to top the overall standings in 1st position. Group B followed in 2nd place with 1 Gold and 3 Silver medals. Group A placed 3rd overall with 1 Gold, 1 Silver and 2 Bronze medals. Group C finished 4th, with a single Bronze medal from the football event.

items.title: 2027 Elections: Army Charges Personnel to Remain Neutral, Professional
items.summary: Chiemelie Ezeobi As Nigeria prepares for the 2027 General Elections, the Nigerian Army has charged its personnel to maintain strict political neutrality, professionalism and respect for the rule of law
items.body: Chiemelie Ezeobi As Nigeria prepares for the 2027 General Elections, the Nigerian Army has charged its personnel to maintain strict political neutrality, professionalism and respect for the rule of law while supporting election security operations. The charge was issued at the 81 Division Nigerian Army Sensitisation Lecture on the Conduct of Armed Forces Personnel during the 2027 General Elections, held on September 1, 2026. The lecture, organised by Headquarters 81 Division, brought together commanders, officers and soldiers of the Nigerian Army, representatives of sister services and other security agencies, as well as resource persons and discussants, to deepen participants’ understanding of the legal and operational responsibilities associated with election security. In his welcome address, the General Officer Commanding (GOC) 81 Division, Major General AA Babalola, said the engagement formed part of the Armed Forces of Nigeria’s commitment to continuous professional development and the responsible discharge of its constitutional responsibilities. According to him, military participation in election security is a constitutionally regulated supporting responsibility undertaken only under lawful authority and prescribed conditions. He reminded personnel that the Armed Forces remain subordinate to constitutionally established civil authority, noting that Sections 217(2)(c) and 218 of the Constitution provide the legal basis for deploying the military in aid of civil authorities when directed by the President. The GOC stressed that every commander and soldier must understand the responsibilities and limitations governing such deployments and strictly comply with lawful directives, approved Rules of Engagement, the Code of Conduct and the established chain of command. Beyond understanding military orders, he said personnel must also be conversant with the Constitution, the Armed Forces Act, the Electoral Act, INEC guidelines, service regulations and other directives governing election security. “Therefore, ignorance of the law cannot be given as an excuse,” he warned, emphasising the consequences of unlawful or unprofessional conduct. The GOC further charged commanders to ensure that deployed personnel understood the lawful thresholds governing searches, arrests, the use of force, the treatment of civilians and the protection of fundamental human rights. While acknowledging the supporting role of the Armed Forces during elections, Major General Babalola emphasised that the Nigeria Police Force remains the primary agency responsible for maintaining public safety and order during elections. He said effective election security would therefore depend on cooperation among participating agencies, adding that tactical success could not be separated from legality, proportionality, restraint and the preservation of public confidence. A major concern highlighted during the engagement was political neutrality. The GOC warned that the neutrality of service personnel must remain “absolute and evident”, stressing that unprofessional conduct by individual personnel could undermine the reputation and credibility of security institutions. The sensitisation lecture also reflected the Command Philosophy of the Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General W Shaibu, which seeks to transform the Nigerian Army into a professional, adaptable, combat-ready and resilient force capable of discharging its constitutional responsibilities within a joint and multi-agency environment. The philosophy, the GOC noted, rests on five pillars: Professional Excellence, Robust Administration, Operational Readiness, Strategic Cooperation and Exemplary Leadership, anchored on a Soldier-First Culture that prioritises personnel welfare, training, dignity, empowerment and institutional credibility. In his opening remarks, the Special Guest of Honour, the Commander, Corps of Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, Major General AO Adereti, similarly stressed the importance of professionalism and constitutional loyalty as the country approaches the elections. He described the sensitisation as a timely and strategically significant engagement designed to strengthen constitutional order, responsible security conduct and confidence in Nigeria’s democratic institutions. According to him, elections increasingly take place within complex security environments characterised by political polarisation, violent extremism, organised crime, cyber threats, misinformation and technology-enabled manipulation. He warned that hate speech, fake news, inflammatory narratives and coordinated attempts to provoke security personnel could heighten tensions and undermine public confidence. For the Armed Forces, he said, the response must be based on intelligence-led planning, strategic communication, institutional cooperation and disciplined action at every level of command. Major General Adereti maintained that the Armed Forces must remain a stabilising national institution whose conduct reassures citizens and reinforces confidence in democratic governance. He therefore urged personnel not to become involved in partisan controversies or engage in actions, associations or public communications capable of suggesting political preference. “Neutrality must be absolute, visible and sustained before, during and after the elections,” he said. He further emphasised that every deployment must be guided by lawful authority, clearly defined responsibilities, approved Rules of Engagement and respect for fundamental human rights. The Special Guest of Honour also underscored the importance of inter-agency cooperation, reiterating that the Nigeria Police Force remains the lead agency for election security and the maintenance of public order, while the Armed Forces and other security agencies operate in supporting capacities underin established constitutional and operational arrangements. For him, the success of election security would depend not only on operational preparedness but also on mutual respect, timely intelligence sharing, a clear understanding of institutional boundaries and seamless coordination. As the lecture progressed, participants were encouraged to examine existing assumptions, ask questions and seek clarification on the legal authorities and operational limitations surrounding military participation in election security. The objective, the GOC said, was to ensure that no uncertainty remained unresolved before personnel were deployed for sensitive national assignments.

items.title: THE CHALLENGE OF JIHADI DRUG CAPTAGON
items.summary: There was something unusual about one of the recent drug interceptions at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport in Lagos. It was not just the quantity involved or the fact that
items.body: There was something unusual about one of the recent drug interceptions at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport in Lagos. It was not just the quantity involved or the fact that the consignment had crossed an international border. It was the name of the drug itself. On August 22, the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) announced the interception of 47,200 tablets of Captagon concealed inside locally made bathing soap, popularly known as Ghana soap. The consignment had arrived from Accra, Ghana, and according to the Agency, the suspect arrested in connection with it said the drugs were intended for northern Nigeria. In separate operations at the same airport, more than 3.9 million tablets of two opioid drugs, Tramaking and Tapentadol, were also recovered. The combined value of the seizures was put at more than ₦6.2 billion. The figure is crazy, but there is another part of the story that deserves our attention. How many Nigerians actually know what Captagon is? For many people, the names that immediately come to mind when drugs are mentioned are cannabis, cocaine, heroin, tramadol and codeine. These are substances that have featured prominently in conversations about drug abuse and trafficking in Nigeria for years. Captagon, however, is not a drug most Nigerians would recognise by name, and that unfamiliarity is precisely why its appearance should not be dismissed as just another seizure. Captagon is an amphetamine-type stimulant that has become prominent in illegal drug markets in parts of the Middle East. Nigeria previously recorded a major interception of the drug in 2021, when more than 451,000 tablets were seized at Apapa Port in Lagos. Its reappearance years later is a reminder that the drug trade is not static. The substances being moved, the routes being used and the methods of concealment can all change. Even the decision to hide the tablets inside bathing soap is instructive. Traffickers do not always need elaborate hiding places. Sometimes, they only need to put something illegal inside something that looks completely ordinary. A box of soap does not attract the same attention as a suspicious-looking package, and that is precisely the kind of thinking that makes modern drug trafficking difficult to tackle. There is a wider concern here for Nigeria. The country already has a significant substance-use problem, with the National Drug Use Survey estimating that 14.3 million Nigerians aged 15 to 64 had used psychoactive substances other than alcohol and tobacco in the year preceding the survey. That means the country cannot afford to wait for every new drug to become popular before beginning to educate people about its dangers. This is particularly important when young people are involved. A teenager cannot make a safe decision about a substance he or she knows nothing about. Parents may warn their children about cannabis or tramadol because those names are familiar, but the drug market is not obliged to remain familiar. New substances can enter through new routes, acquire new street names and find new users before families and communities fully understand what is happening. The interception also shows why Nigeria’s drug problem cannot be considered only within its own borders. A consignment travelling from Ghana to Nigeria is part of a regional trafficking network. The people involved may operate in different countries, while the drugs themselves can move through several locations before reaching their intended market. This requires countries in the region to share intelligence and work together, because a weakness in one country’s border can quickly become a problem for another. But stopping consignments is only one part of the answer. There must also be attention to the people financing these operations, the networks arranging the movement of the drugs and the demand that keeps the business profitable. At the same time, prevention and public education have to keep pace with the changing drug market. Perhaps the biggest lesson from the Captagon seizure is that Nigerians should not assume that the drugs we know today are the only drugs we will have to worry about tomorrow. By the time an unfamiliar substance becomes common enough for everybody to know its name, it may already have found a market. The real challenge, therefore, is not simply to keep stopping the drugs that have already become familiar. It is to see the next threat early, understand it quickly and prevent it from becoming another problem that Nigeria wishes it had taken seriously sooner. Janet Udoh, Uyo, Akwa Ibom

items.title: LESSONS FROM NEPAL’S FLOOD DISASTER
items.summary: Government should invest heavily in flood prevention The people of Nepal are still counting their losses from the devastating flash flood which ripped through their border with China, inundating towns,
items.body: Government should invest heavily in flood prevention The people of Nepal are still counting their losses from the devastating flash flood which ripped through their border with China, inundating towns, crushing roads and bridges and causing the death of more than a thousand people in its path. The last time Nigeria witnessed this type of extremely shocking flooding was in 2012 which killed no fewer than 363 people, displaced about three million others and about 600,000 houses either damaged or destroyed. But following the tragedy in Nepal, the Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMET), Nigerian Hydrological Services Agency (NIHSA) are concerned that the 2012 flooding could happen again if their warnings continue to be ignored. The National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) also enjoins Nigerians to remain vigilant because such a devastating flooding can occur with little notice. Recurring flood disasters in the country are no longer isolated seasonal incidents but a growing national crisis demanding urgent action on urban planning, drainage, early warning systems and public preparedness. But the most disturbing aspect of Nigeria’s flood crisis is not that flooding occurs. It is that authorities and citizens largely know where the risks are located, but continue to allow development, particularly in highbrow estates. Yet government cannot simultaneously warn citizens against building on waterways and permit developments that obstruct free flow of water. Where planning authorities approve construction in flood-prone areas, responsibility does not rest solely with the property owner. The approving authority must also answer for the consequences. This is why Nigeria’s physical planning system requires urgent reform. Land allocation and building approvals must no longer be treated primarily as administrative exercises. Every proposed development in a flood-sensitive area should be subjected to credible environmental assessments before approval. The government must also stop the practice of allowing development to precede infrastructure. No serious city can continue approving buildings without ensuring adequate drainage, storm-water channels, road network and waste-management systems. Nigerians, too, must exercise greater responsibility by carrying out due diligence before purchasing land and building on it. What the tragedy in Nepal also teaches is that early warnings must be more than technical forecasts. A villager, trader, commuter or resident does not need complicated meteorological terminology. People need to know whether they are at risk, when the danger is expected, what action they should take, and where they can seek safety. Government at all levels should therefore establish clear standards for issuing and disseminating flood alerts, including the use of telecommunications networks, radio, television, social media, community leaders and local emergency structures. More importantly, Nigeria needs to invest in prevention rather than continually spending heavily on response. Every naira spent clearing a blocked drainage channel before the rains is potentially money saved from emergency reconstruction after a flood. Every illegal structure prevented from obstructing a waterway may save lives and millions of naira in property losses. The federal and state governments must make flood prevention a measurable component of urban governance. Governments must embark on sustained drainage rehabilitation and maintenance rather than seasonal desilting exercises conducted only after flooding begins. Development approvals must be linked to environmental and flood-risk assessments, with no exceptions for politically connected developers or property owners. Floods may be natural events, but the destruction they cause is often amplified by human decisions. Nigeria cannot prevent every rainfall-induced disaster. It can, however, prevent people from building on waterways, stop drains from becoming refuse dumps, enforce planning regulations, improve warning systems and prepare communities before the water arrives. The choice is no longer between flooding and lack of flooding. It is between preparedness and catastrophe. With the Nepal floods, Nigeria has been warned. It must act now by strengthening real-time hydrological monitoring and establishing binding information-sharing arrangements with neighbouring countries, particularly on major transboundary rivers and dams.

items.title: 2027: Sanwo-Olu, Hamzat urge peaceful elections

items.body: — Lagos APC vows full mobilisation for Tinubu, Hamzat, candidates By Olasunkanmi Akoni LAGOS — Ahead of the 2027 general elections, Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu of Lagos State, his deputy, Dr Obafemi Hamzat, and leaders of the All Progressives Congress, APC, have urged residents to shun violence and ensure peaceful conduct before, during and after the polls. They made the call on Tuesday at an interdenominational prayer session for the re-election of President Bola Tinubu, the election of Hamzat as Lagos State governor and other APC candidates, held at the Mobolaji Johnson Arena, Onikan, Lagos Island. The prayer session, attended by party leaders, supporters and religious faithful, was organised to seek divine guidance, commit the party’s electoral aspirations to God and formally commence mobilisation for the 2027 elections. Among those at the event were Senator Musiliu Obanikoro; Speaker of the Lagos State House of Assembly, Mudashiru Obasa; former Speaker of the House, Adeyemi Ikuforiji; Pa Tajudeen Olusi; Senator Ganiu Solomon; Jumoke Okoya-Thomas; Senator Idiat Adebule; Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Wale Edun; APC Lagos Chairman, Pastor Cornelius Ojelabi; Fouad Oki; members of the National Assembly and state House of Assembly; members of Conference 57 comprising 20 local government chairmen and 37 Local Council Development Area chairmen, as well as traditional rulers and religious leaders. Speaking at the event, Sanwo-Olu stressed the importance of laying a spiritual foundation ahead of political activities. He said the party would combine prayer with grassroots mobilisation and engagement with voters across the state. Sanwo-Olu said although the party was relying on prayer, its members were also conscious that “faith without work is dead.” He said the APC would not take any voter, community or stakeholder for granted, adding that the party planned to take its campaign to communities across the 20 local government areas and 37 LCDAs of the state. According to him, the party’s objectives include securing the re-election of President Tinubu and victory for its National Assembly and state-level candidates. Sanwo-Olu also pledged his support for Hamzat and his running mate, Damilola James-Sonayon, urging party members and residents to ensure that the electoral process remained peaceful and free from violence. He further pledged to participate in the national presidential campaign to support the party’s efforts ahead of the election. The governor prayed for a peaceful and prosperous Nigeria, stressing the need for unity and national development. Also speaking, Hamzat said the prayer session provided an opportunity to commit the party’s candidates and the electoral process to God. He prayed for peaceful elections without clashes, accidents or loss of lives, while expressing confidence in the prospects of APC candidates. Hamzat also expressed confidence in the party’s candidates contesting the three senatorial seats, 24 House of Representatives seats and 40 Lagos State House of Assembly seats. Earlier, the Director-General of the Kadiri Obafemi Hamzat, KOH, Campaign Council, Senator Musiliu Obanikoro, said the prayer was necessary because human efforts alone could not determine the outcome of every circumstance. Obanikoro urged party members to place the interest of the APC above personal ambitions, warning that internal disagreements should not weaken the party ahead of the elections. He called for dialogue, reconciliation, discipline and unity among candidates and supporters, urging them to campaign with respect and focus on their capacity to serve the people. Obanikoro said the campaign organisation would take the APC’s message to communities across Lagos State and the wider South-West. He expressed confidence that the APC would emerge victorious in the presidential, National Assembly and state elections, particularly projecting the emergence of Hamzat as governor and Damilola Sonayon James as deputy governor. The event featured prayers by Christian, Muslim and traditional worshippers for Tinubu, Hamzat, other APC candidates and the peaceful conduct of the 2027 elections. items.title: Atiku’s war on Nigeria’s mandate

items.body: By Emma Chinedu There is a kind of childishness that comes over Nigerian politics whenever power is at stake, a pretence that we are searching for angels to govern us when every serious country in the world knows that leadership belongs to flawed human beings, drawn from the same history, weaknesses and contradictions as the people they seek to lead. Nigeria is no exception, yet the opposition has once again walked away from the hard work of democratic persuasion and begun scouring foreign files and offices for scraps it can turn into a fresh political weapon against an opponent. The relentless campaign by ADC candidate Atiku Abubakar to press for the release and publicise decades-old files in the custody of the United States Federal Bureau of Investigation concerning President Bola Ahmed Tinubu is the latest manifestation of this syndrome. Atiku presents this cross-border campaign in the noble language of public interest and the right to know. But its political intent is clearly to reopen in Washington a verdict he could not overturn in Nigeria. That is lawfare by other means. Atiku wants American agencies to furnish the material for a permanent campaign of suspicion against the Tinubu presidency, as if Nigerian institutions, Nigerian courts and Nigerian votes were not enough. No democracy operates on the expectation of angelic leadership. If Nigerians are looking for flawless rulers, they will have to search for them in heaven. No society rises above itself. Its leaders come from the same country, the same history and the same human condition as the people they lead. The United States, whose files Atiku treats as a moral oracle, offers a particularly unforgiving lesson. Donald Trump went into the 2024 election with 34 felony convictions returned by a New York jury after a public criminal trial. For years, state and federal investigations had shadowed his public life, while the global media dissected every filing and courtroom turn, expecting American voters to recoil in moral horror. His record lay before them in open court and in the public record, yet they made their own judgement and returned him to the White House. He was sworn in as President because voters judged the whole man, his record, his capacity, the direction he offered and the country’s interests as they saw them. Atiku should understand what that means. His path to the Nigerian presidency does not run through Washington or an FBI docket. It runs through Nigerian voters, and he must persuade them that he has a better answer to the country’s future. If the United States, with all its power and moral posturing, can separate a leader’s legal history from his present mandate, why should Nigeria impose on itself a harsher standard? Why must a Nigerian leader be an unblemished angel before his voters may judge him fit to govern? Is that not the height of democratic unseriousness? How did we acquire this wretched habit of looking outside ourselves for standards that even the West does not live by? Atiku has chosen to feed that weakness, issuing press releases that leave the impression that Washington is sitting on a smoking gun, one that will decide the next election before Nigerians get to decide it for themselves. That is the illusion being sold. All the heat around these FBI files comes back to a civil asset forfeiture case in Chicago more than thirty years old. It was a civil case. It did not produce a criminal conviction. Yet Atiku’s people want Nigerians to read it as though it were one. These facts have not changed in thirty years. They are neither new nor secret, and they do not disqualify Tinubu under the law. Yet Atiku is trying to pass off these thirty-year-old administrative echoes as fresh, damning revelations. He has hired Washington lobbyists, including Von Batten-Montague-York, to circulate the documents among Capitol Hill staff and international journalists. It is a fishing expedition. The point is to lift snippets of investigative prose, unverified interview notes and agency chatter out of their setting, then build a case for moral disqualification where no legal disqualification exists. Raw malice drives this Washington campaign, a deliberate effort to keep a cloud over the presidency and make Nigeria look like a permanent scandal in the eyes of the world because Atiku cannot accept that the Nigerian electorate has r epeatedly refused to hand him the presidency. If he cannot rule Nigeria, then he will do everything in his power to make its elected leader appear illegitimate. That is the scorched-earth politics he has chosen, putting personal vindication ahead of national stability The most offensive thing about this multi-million-dollar Washington campaign is the contempt it shows for Nigerian democratic institutions and for Nigerian voters themselves. Tinubu’s background, identity and legal history have been in public view for a quarter of a century. They were on the table when he ran for Governor of Lagos in 1999 and again in 2003. They were on the table throughout his years at the centre of the progressive opposition, and they were argued in public and in court before, during and after the 2023 presidential election. None of this surfaced yesterday. Nigerians knew the arguments before they voted. Nigeria does not have to go to Washington to vet its leaders. INEC cleared Tinubu. The Code of Conduct Bureau examined him. The Presidential Election Petition Tribunal heard the opposition’s case, weighed the certified documents and dismissed their objections. The Supreme Court , the final and absolute arbiter of our constitutional democracy, reviewed the matter and affirmed his mandate. When Atiku Abubakar takes this fight to Washington and asks the FBI and DEA for material to deploy against Tinubu ahead of 2027, he is telling the world that the judgement Nigerians made in 2023 can be discredited from abroad, and that the next election should be shaped by whatever a foreign agency releases rather than by the case the candidates make before Nigerians. Put plainly, he wants a file in Washington to do the work of persuading voters at home. Democracy is a contract between the leader and the led, not between a candidate and a foreign intelligence agency. Nigerians made their judgement in 2023 after weighing the candidates, their records and their promises; in 2027, they will make another. Atiku’s task is to persuade them that he deserves that next verdict, not to use a thirty-year-old civil matter in Washington to write the result before the campaign is fought. Tinubu has a country to govern. He is dealing with economic distortions left by years of decay, while trying to steady the monetary system, attract investment, expand infrastructure and steer Nigeria through a difficult global economy. It is hard work, and Nigerians will judge it by what they see in their lives, not by what Washington lobbyists choose to circulate. Atiku will say his latest campaign is about the cost of living, and he has even promised to restore petrol subsidy despite arguing in 2023 that it was unsustainable; but that only exposes the contradiction at the centre of his campaign, because when Nigerians worry about inflation, food, transport and jobs, his answer is to turn archived American court dockets into a campaign weapon abroad while promising at home to return the country to the same subsidy regime he once said Nigeria could not sustain. Indeed, we are witnessing the last-ditch politics of a man prepared to say whatever he thinks might carry him into Aso Rock. The FBI records saga will run its course, the files will be reviewed and the lawyers will have their say, but no pile of paperwork from Washington can give Atiku the political breakthrough he has spent years failing to secure before Nigerians, or settle 2027 before Nigerians have spoken. What will remain is the record of who stood for Nigeria and who stood against her dignity. Leave the hunt for angels to theologians. Nations are governed by leaders who take hard decisions, bear the consequences and submit themselves to the judgement of their people. Bola Ahmed Tinubu is the democratically elected President of a sovereign Federal Republic. His mandate belongs to Nigerians, and in 2027 it will be renewed or rejected by Nigerians, not by a file in Washington. • Chinedu is a public affairs analyst based in Enugu The post Atiku’s war on Nigeria’s mandate appeared first on The Sun Nigeria .

items.body: —As VP Shettima directs relevant stakeholders, agencies to develop roadmap for NEC’s endorsement By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ABUJA— THE Federal Government on Tuesday, directed stakeholders and relevant agencies to design a comprehensive operational roadmap for the nationwide rollout of the 112 national emergency number. Accordingly, it constituted a committee comprising the Nigeria Police Force (NPF), the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC), and other relevant agencies to finalise the roadmap and standard operating procedures for formal endorsement of the National Economic Council (NEC). Recall that NEC had recently approved the 112 as Nigeria’s single universal toll-free emergency number to replace fragmented and slow response lines, with a view to eliminating bureaucratic red tape and allow citizens easy access to rapid help during fires, accidents, medical crises, or security breaches. Speaking in Abuja during the National Emergency Number 112 Project stakeholders meeting, the Vice President who gave the directive, urged the committee to ensure their decisions are based on global best practises in order to have a clear roadmap. Charging the committee to finalize the roadmap and standard operating procedures for formal NEC endorsement, Senator Shettima stressed the need to make significant progress, assuring that once it becomes visible, resources will be available to fund the process. “Let’s make progress so that whatever time we have spent here is worth spending. And most importantly, the engine is finance. It is resources to drive the process. And I want to assure you that we will get the resources,” he stated. On his part, the Inspector General of Police (IGP), Olatunji Rilwan Disu, said the Nigeria Police Force was fully in support of the adoption of 112 as Nigeria’s unified national emergency number. From an operational perspective, he noted that it is “a significant step towards ensuring that citizens have a simple and reliable means of accessing emergency assistance.” He explained that for a citizen facing an armed attack, accident, fire outbreak, medical emergency, kidnapping, or any other life-threatening situation, while the first challenge is to determine which agency to call, one number should provide access to the appropriate response. Earlier in her presentation, the Personal Assistant to the President on e-Governance (Office of the Vice President), Mrs. Lydia Aina, noted that emergency response in Nigeria runs across many agencies, systems, and jurisdictions, creating fragmentation in how emergencies are received, coordinated, and responded to. The goal, she said, is to move from the fragmented states through coordinated response to a fully integrated national framework, just as she explained that the meeting was about the system behind the process, including “the people, the agencies, the standards that make the number actually work when citizens dial it. “Our job now is to turn it into an actual working programme with milestones. So, we have identified six immediate priorities. First, governance. We need a clear structure of who’s responsible for what,” she explained. Other stakeholders who pledged the full support of their agencies at the meeting included the Director-General of NEMA, Mrs. Zubaida Umar; Corps Marshal of FRSC, Shehu Mohammed, and Director-General of the National Orientation Agency (NOA), Mallam Lanre Issa-Onilu, among others. items.title: Govt officials stealing from the poor: How far can Falana’s advocacy go?
items.summary: Human rights lawyer, Femi Falana, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria, SAN, has scored another plus as he called on the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to investigate the alleged failure of the Federal Government of Nigeria “to account for N33.75 billion earmarked for cash transfers to vulnerable or poor Nigerians.” The post Govt officials stealing from the poor: How far can Falana’s advo
items.body: By Samuel Egburonu Human rights lawyer, Femi Falana, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria, SAN, has scored another plus as he called on the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to investigate the alleged failure of the Federal Government of Nigeria “to account for N33.75 billion earmarked for cash transfers to vulnerable or poor Nigerians.” It has, for years now, remained one of the most shameful realities of our country that some of the most lucrative ministries or agencies for corrupt government officials have remained ministries or agencies officially set up to cater for the humanitarian needs of the poor, the hungry and the internally displaced victims of our society. You will shed real hot tears if you witness the passion with which government officials lobby to be posted to such ministries and agencies, and if you know that the passion is not borne out of love to help the poor but to steal from the helpless needy. It has become an open secret that the billions of naira constantly voted for disbursement to poor and hungry Nigerians through these ministries and agencies, do not get to them. Yes, at every seminar or official outing, government officials gleefully quote billions of naira allegedly used to take care of the Nigerian poor. But we all know it has always been and has remained a wicked joke, a lie no one is really ashamed of or ready to fight against. This is why Falana’s latest advocacy, in the interest of the poor citizens, is worthy of our commendationhere. Falana, who chairs the Alliance on Surviving COVID-19 and Beyond (ASCAB), did not only raise that alarm but urged EFCC, Nigeria’s anti- graft agency, to collaborate with the Auditor-General of the Federation (AuGF) to recover the funds if investigations establish they were diverted. Falana made this call in a statement on Sunday, following concerns raised in the Auditor-General’s 2024 Annual Report on Non-Compliance/Internal Control Weaknesses in Ministries, Departments and Agencies of the Federal Government. According to the report, “the Federal Government was unable to provide adequate evidence showing that N33.75 billion in cash transfers reached the intended beneficiaries.” According to Falana, “the funds were meant to support more than 3.29 million vulnerable households under the National Social Investment Programme.” He described the situation as “particularly disturbing given measures introduced by the government to improve beneficiary tracking and prevent the inclusion of fictitious beneficiaries in the social intervention programmes. “The National Social Investment Programme Agency (NSIPA), established under the NSIPA Act 2022, oversees major federal social intervention schemes, including N-Power, the National Home-Grown School Feeding Programme, the National Cash Transfer Programme and the National Social Safety Net Programme.” As Falana noted, NSIPA and its predecessor agencies had faced several allegations of financial impropriety involving government officials.” He recalled that former Minister of Humanitarian Affairs, Disaster Management and Social Development, Sadiya Umar Farouq, was investigated by the EFCC over alleged money laundering involving more than N37.1 billion. He also referred to the suspension of former Humanitarian Affairs Minister, Betta Edu, in December 2023 following a directive involving the transfer of N585 million in public intervention funds to a private bank account. Falana further recalled that the former National Coordinator and Chief Executive Officer of NSIPA, Halima Shehu, was suspended and questioned over alleged suspicious financial transactions. He called on the EFCC to conclude investigations into the various allegations and to make the results of its findings public. “The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission should liaise with the Auditor-General of the Federation with a view to recovering the missing N33.75 billion,” Falana said. He also called for the immediate investigation of what he described as a serious allegation involving the possible diversion of funds meant for poor and vulnerable Nigerians. “All the characters involved in the shameful conduct should be arrested and prosecuted without any delay,” he said. I totally agree with this Learned Silk. The point is that cheats in humanitarian ministries and agencies in Nigeria should be singled out and delt with for the damage they have so far done to Nigerian governments and to the people can no longer be easily quantified. It is wicked enough to steal public resources put in the care of an individual. But when that public resource is specifically meant to be used to save the lives of dying, hungry and poor elements in the society, it is obviously inhuman for the rich elements put in trust of such funds to be the same thieves that would so callously appropriate the public resources. This explains why we must take this particular betrayal more seriously. In my view, our laws should specifically provide for exemplary punishment in such circumstances to at least discourage this level of inhumanity and wickedness against Nigeria and against her people. It must be stated here that the current Nigerian government has not done well enough to convince the people it is not actually behind the grand scheme of ripping off the poor in this fashion. For example, Falana also expressed “concern over the implementation of a $3.05 billion development programme unveiled by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu in July 2026.” Reports said the “package, backed by the World Bank, is designed to support poverty reduction, human capital development and expanded economic opportunities.” Falana “urged the Federal Government to strengthen accountability measures to ensure that funds allocated for poverty reduction reach their intended beneficiaries.” He also proposed the establishment of an independent monitoring body comprising credible civil society organisations to oversee the disbursement and implementation of the development funds. He pointed out that “stronger oversight was necessary to prevent public officials from misappropriating resources intended to assist Nigerians living in poverty and other vulnerable groups.” Falana’s concerns here are easy to understand or appreciate for the bitter image of hungry Nigerians bursting open rice-filled locked warehouses during the recent protests against hunger in Nigeria is still vivid in people’s memories. Untill today, it is still difficult to fully understand why well fed politicians and top civil servants would collaborate to hide in huge warehouses food and other humanitarian provisions meant for dying citizens and watch them die slowly while government continue to claim it has adequately provided for the people? The question that still remains unanswered is whether the action of hiding the food was meant to starve the people to death or to portray the government as wicked? The deepest puzzle to me remains why the government, after discovery of the grand betrayal, would allow it’s officials who stole or tried to steal so heartlessly from the poor, to go home unpunished after presenting the government as uncaring and unperforming? It would be necessary for all of us to consider what kind of message such a government would be leaving behind? Or is it that nobody in Aso Rock really bothers about these concerns? As would be expected from everything Nigerian, it may be more realistic to expect that many experts will soon offer their services to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu-led Federal Government to help fault Falana’s current advocacy. They will advice Mr President not to allow his political opponents to portray his government in bad light ahead of 2027 Presidential Election. That has always been the pattern. May I however advice President Tinubu not to be deceived by such jaundiced advice for it can never be in his interest and in the interest of his government if all the billions claims he has voted for the feeding of Nigerian poor and the vulnerable have always been diverted by theives that claim to be working for him and for his government. So, as Falana suggested, time has come for EFCC to truly investigate the reports of such callous diversions and to make the results of the investigations public. If this is done now and before 2027 Elections, it will expose the real theives and benefit all of us common Nigerians • Samuel Hezekiah Egburonu Esq, A Veteran Journalist And Lawyer Is A Public Affairs Analyst The post Govt officials stealing from the poor: How far can Falana’s advocacy go? appeared first on The Sun Nigeria .

items.title: Flood alert
items.summary: For the men who dive where others fear to look, every rainy season is a race against time as well as against death. As dark clouds gather over Kaduna State and the annual rains begin to swell the Kaduna River, a familiar anxiety returns to communities living along its banks. The post Flood alert appeared first on The Sun Nigeria .
items.body: Kaduna River divers vigilant, receive life jackets donation as state government reaffirms commitment to protecting life and property through coordinated sensitization programmes and disaster response initiatives From Noah Ebije, Kaduna For the men who dive where others fear to look, every rainy season is a race against time as well as against death. As dark clouds gather over Kaduna State and the annual rains begin to swell the Kaduna River, a familiar anxiety returns to communities living along its banks. For decades, the river has been both a blessing and a tragedy. It provides water, supports livelihoods and defines parts of Kaduna’s landscape. But, every rainy season, it transforms into a dangerous force, swallowing roads, destroying homes and, too often, claiming lives. Long before emergency agencies arrive, there is usually another group already in the water. Barefoot, armed with little more than courage and experience, local divers plunge into the muddy currents searching for missing persons, rescuing stranded residents and recovering victims swept away by the floodwaters. Their silent sacrifice received rare recognition recently. On the banks of Kaduna River, the Women Wing leader of the Peace Revival and Reconciliation Foundation of Nigeria (PRRFN), Hajiya Ramatu Tijjani, distributed life jackets to local divers and volunteer rescuers as part of efforts to prepare them for another challenging flood season. The donation may appear simple, but for the divers, it could mean the difference between returning home safely after a rescue operation or becoming victims themselves. “This is about protecting those who protect others,” Hajiya Ramatu said while handing over the safety equipment at the riverbank. She described the divers as unsung heroes whose commitment has saved countless lives during floods and water-related emergencies across Kaduna State. According to her, their work extends beyond flood rescue. She revealed that the divers have also intervened in several cases involving people attempting suicide by jumping into the river, often linked to economic hardship and mental health challenges. “They deserve national honour because of the important role they play in saving lives,” she said. She appealed to wealthy individuals, corporate organisations and humanitarian groups to support the volunteer rescuers with additional life jackets, ropes, rescue boats and other emergency equipment. The philanthropist also announced plans to extend similar support to divers operating around Zaria as part of broader efforts to strengthen community-based emergency response across Kaduna State. The Kaduna River has shaped the history of the state for generations. Flowing through Kaduna metropolis before joining the Niger River, it has repeatedly overflowed its banks during periods of heavy rainfall, particularly when intense downpours coincide with releases from upstream water bodies. Communities such as Kabala Costain, Unguwan Rimi, Kigo Road, Kudenda, parts of Kakuri and several settlements around the river have experienced flooding at different times over the years. Major floods have displaced thousands of residents, submerged homes and damaged roads, bridges and farmlands. In recent years, changing weather patterns linked to climate change have made flooding increasingly unpredictable, with experts warning that heavier rainfall events are becoming more frequent across Nigeria. The situation often leaves local communities relying on volunteer divers before formal rescue agencies can fully mobilise. Despite the dangers they face, many of the divers have continued their work without basic protective equipment. Most rely on personal swimming skills acquired from childhood and years of navigating the river. When floods occur, they respond immediately; often diving repeatedly into fast-moving water where visibility is almost zero. For many of them, every rescue operation is a gamble with death. Receiving the life jackets, therefore, brought both relief and renewed hope. Speaking on behalf of the divers, Mallam Dattijo Gada, expressed gratitude to Hajiya Ramatu Tijjani for recognising their sacrifices. He prayed for God’s blessings upon the philanthropist and said the donation would significantly improve their safety while carrying out rescue operations. He noted that dozens of divers working around the Kaduna Bridge still lack life jackets and urgently require more protective equipment. According to him, additional support would enable the team to respond more effectively whenever flood emergencies occur. “Our work is to save lives, we have rescued many people who accidentally fell into the river, and during floods we are usually among the first responders,” Gada said. Emergency management experts have repeatedly warned that communities located near rivers across Nigeria remain increasingly vulnerable as rainfall patterns become more intense. Each year, authorities encourage residents in flood-prone areas to relocate temporarily whenever flood alerts are issued. Yet despite government interventions, local volunteers continue to provide the first line of response in many communities. Their knowledge of the river’s currents, hidden channels and dangerous depths often proves invaluable during rescue missions. The event was more than the distribution of safety equipment because for many observers, it represented long-overdue recognition of ordinary citizens who quietly risk everything for complete strangers. As another rainy season unfolds, the Kaduna River will likely continue its age-old cycle, nourishing communities one moment and threatening them the next. But along its banks, where floodwaters often turn panic into tragedy, a group of determined divers now stand slightly better prepared. Wearing newly donated life jackets instead of relying solely on courage, they remain ready to answer the call whenever the river rises, because when the flood comes, they know the first life they save may depend on protecting their own. Also, over the years, the Nigerian Red Cross Society has remained one of the leading humanitarian organisations responding to flood disasters in Kaduna State and across Nigeria. Whenever the Kaduna River bursts its banks, Red Cross volunteers are often deployed alongside officials of the National Emergency Management Agency and the Kaduna State Emergency Management Agency to evacuate vulnerable residents, administer first aid, reunite separated families and distribute relief materials to displaced persons. Their intervention has become particularly critical following devastating floods recorded in recent years, when hundreds of households were forced from their homes by rising water levels. However, beyond emergency rescue, the organisation regularly conducts community sensitization campaigns on flood preparedness, early warning systems and safe evacuation procedures in vulnerable communities along the Kaduna River. Humanitarian experts said the work of volunteer divers complements these formal emergency efforts. While agencies coordinate large-scale rescue operations and relief, local divers are usually the first to respond because they understand the river’s currents, hidden channels and dangerous depths better than anyone else. It is this partnership between trained humanitarian organisations and community volunteers that has helped save countless lives over the years. As climate change continues to increase the frequency and intensity of flooding across Nigeria, experts believe strengthening both institutional emergency response and grassroots rescue capacity will be essential to reducing future flood-related deaths. As flooding looms in Kaduna, it is believed that the donated life jackets are part of a wider network of flood preparedness involving both professional humanitarian responders and the community divers who are often the first to enter the water. Meanwhile, Kaduna State Government has intensified efforts to raise public awareness and strengthen emergency preparedness following the 2026 seasonal climate prediction released by the Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet), which identified Kaduna as one of the states vulnerable to flooding due to expected above-normal rainfall during the 2026 rainy season. According to the state Commissioner for Information and Culture, Ahmed Maiyaki, the government has reaffirmed its commitment to protecting lives and property through coordinated sensitization programmes and disaster response initiatives across the state. The NiMet forecast indicates that rainfall in Kaduna State is expected to begin between May 19 and June 10, 2026, while the rainy season is projected to end between October 5 and October 21, 2026. The forecast also warned of a possible severe 21-day dry spell between June and August, a condition that could further increase the risk of flooding and other environmental challenges. items.title: Land dispute threatens peace in Ogun community as residents seek urgent government intervention
items.summary: A simmering land dispute in Obakobe and adjoining Ogu-speaking communities in Ado Odo/Ota Local Government Area of Ogun State is threatening to disrupt the relative peace in the area, with residents alleging repeated encroachment, harassment, destruction of property and attacks by suspected land grabbers. items.body: A simmering land dispute in Obakobe and adjoining Ogu-speaking communities in Ado Odo/Ota Local Government Area of Ogun State is threatening to disrupt the relative peace in the area, with residents alleging repeated encroachment, harassment, destruction of property and attacks by suspected land grabbers. The residents have consequently appealed to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun, security agencies, the Ogun State Bureau of Lands and Survey and traditional authorities to urgently intervene and prevent the dispute from degenerating into a communal crisis. •Victims The aggrieved residents insist that the matter should be resolved strictly through the law, arguing that continued confrontation over land could further endanger lives and livelihoods in the affected communities. According to them, the Ogu people are indigenous to Obakobe, where they have lived for generations, with farming and trading constituting major sources of livelihood. Speaking with journalists, Sonayon Olaoluwa, a Professor of Diaspora and Transnational Studies, University of Ibadan and member of the Steering Committee of the Ogu General Assembly, said the majority of the indigenous population of Obakobe were Ogu people who had lived in the area for several centuries. Olaoluwa alleged that suspected land grabbers had repeatedly invaded the communities despite the provisions of the Ogun State Anti-Land Grabbing Law of 2016. He claimed that the alleged incursions had resulted in harassment of residents, destruction of CCTV cameras, theft of livestock and motorcycles and other acts of violence. “This is no longer just a conventional land ownership dispute. The government must investigate these allegations and ensure that every claim to the land is determined through due legal process,” he said. Olaoluwa specifically mentioned someone, whom he described as the latest land grabber and claimed that he was engaged by some people to cause unrest in the community. “These land grabbers are not our community leaders; they are not Baales. We do not know them. The government must investigate their identities and establish the basis of their claims to the land,” he said. The allegations against the named individuals could not be independently verified as of press time, while those mentioned were not available for comment. Olaoluwa also referred to an existing Court of Appeal judgment which, according to him, favoured the Ogu community. He argued that any party dissatisfied with the judgment should seek appropriate judicial remedies rather than resort to intimidation, harassment or confrontation. He further raised concerns over a separate land dispute involving individuals from a neighbouring community, alleging that a judgment concerning land located several villages away was being relied upon to assert ownership over portions of land in Obakobe. According to him, the legal basis for extending such a judgment to Obakobe should be carefully examined, particularly where, he alleged, residents of the community were not parties to the original proceedings. The community representative also called on the authorities to verify the ownership documents, survey records and boundaries relating to hectares of land allegedly being claimed by some people. Olaoluwa also questioned an alleged claim by an individual to a traditional leadership position in the community, urging relevant authorities to establish the legitimacy of the title and determine whether it had any bearing on land ownership. Those allegations could not be independently verified. A native of the community, Jimoh Abamo, recalled an alleged attack in 2012 in which a young man was injured. He said the incident created such fear that some parents withdrew their children from school over concerns about their safety. He said the parties subsequently reached a peace agreement under which separate portions of land were allocated to them, but alleged that the agreement was no longer being respected. “We reported these incidents to the Ado Odo police division, but no meaningful action was taken. Instead, they kept detaining our people. It is difficult to understand why law enforcement would protect individuals accused of invading another community,” he alleged. Abamo warned that continued destruction of property and alleged attacks could trigger unrest if the government failed to intervene. “We do not want to take the law into our own hands. That is why we are making this public appeal and asking the government and the Olofin of Ado-Odo Kingdom, Oba Olusola Idris Adebowale Lamidi-Osolo (Otenibotemole II), to intervene promptly,” he said. Another resident, who spoke anonymously, described the atmosphere in the community as increasingly tense. “We have lived in this community for generations, and we have never experienced anything like this. Now, strangers have come, claiming ownership of our land, yet we do not know them,” the resident said. Documents made available to journalists indicated that a court order of perpetual injunction was reportedly issued restraining further encroachment beyond previously agreed boundaries. The residents, however, alleged that encroachment and attacks had continued intermittently despite the reported order. They called on the Ogun State Government to review any disputed gazette, summon all relevant stakeholders and work with judicial, traditional and security authorities to establish the facts and resolve the dispute. Beyond the land dispute, the residents expressed concern over what they described as years of infrastructural neglect in the affected communities. They cited poor roads, inadequate electricity supply and limited access to healthcare as major challenges confronting the people. For the residents, the land dispute has therefore compounded existing socio-economic difficulties and heightened fears over the safety of people, homes and livelihoods. They urged the government to protect lives and property, investigate all allegations without prejudice and ensure that no individual or group is allowed to take the law into its own hands. The residents also appealed to the media to continue highlighting the situation, insisting that their objective was not confrontation but a peaceful and lawful resolution. They reaffirmed their commitment to dialogue, the rule of law and peaceful coexistence, but warned that the situation required urgent attention before a dispute over land escalated into a wider communal crisis. For now, the people of Obakobe are asking for one thing: intervention before tension gives way to violence.Land dispute threatens peace in Ogun community as residents seek urgent government intervention.
