items.title: Opinion | VP Nyandeng’s critique and the splintered politics of South Sudan
items.summary: It has become increasingly clear that South Sudan’s political climate remains shadowed by the events The post Opinion | VP Nyandeng’s critique and the splintered politics of South Sudan appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: It has become increasingly clear that South Sudan’s political climate remains shadowed by the events of December 2013, when an internal power struggle within the ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM) fractured the country. Over the past decade, regional mediators and external actors have pursued various party-integration initiatives, most notably the 2015 Arusha Reunification Agreement. Yet recent political tensions, highlighted by controversial remarks from Vice President Rebecca Nyandeng de Mabior, also a member of the SPLM Political Bureau, suggest that beneath the veneer of institutional unity, many of the grievances, suspicions and unresolved structural questions of 2013 remain deeply rooted within the party’s leadership. To understand the volatile reactions to recent political developments, it is necessary to examine the fragmentation that followed the 2013 crisis. While the armed rebellion led by then-First Vice President Riek Machar evolved into the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in-Opposition (SPLM-IO), operating as a separate political entity, the internal struggle over the direction of the original party remained a distinct battleground. That internal contest primarily involved the party establishment under President Salva Kiir Mayardit and the SPLM Former Detainees, a group of senior political figures commonly known as the G-10 who were detained at the outset of the conflict. By avoiding the armed rebellion, the Former Detainees positioned themselves as a political and technocratic alternative, seeking to influence and reform the ruling party without taking up arms against it. For years, the official narrative from the SPLM has emphasized formal mechanisms of reconciliation aimed at repairing this internal rift. Various diplomatic initiatives, from consultations in Tanzania to declarations in Cairo, sought to reintegrate the Former Detainees into the broader party structure as part of efforts to stabilize the country. Yet subsequent developments have shown that formal party reunification does not necessarily resolve an underlying struggle for political power. Factional identities have not been systematically dismantled. Instead, they appear to have been temporarily contained by the imperatives of elite survival and transitional governance. The fragile nature of this political settlement became evident following a public address by Vice President Rebecca Nyandeng de Mabior during a memorial service for the late veteran politician Kosti Manibe. Nyandeng, widow of South Sudan’s founding president, Dr John Garang de Mabior, and a prominent figure historically associated with the Former Detainees, criticized the performance of the current administration. She questioned the effectiveness of governance, challenged the nature of the advisory structures surrounding President Kiir and lamented what she described as the marginalization of those who fought for the country’s liberation. Her remarks resonated because they revived some of the grievances associated with the 2013 crisis: frustration over executive centralization, institutional stagnation and the perceived exclusion of historical liberation figures from meaningful decision-making. The backlash that followed, however, exposed divisions over how internal dissent should be handled. Initially, the Former Detainees’ parliamentary chief whip in the Transitional National Legislative Assembly, Isaiah Hakim Garang, held a press conference in which he rebuked the vice president. He accused her of political incitement and said her remarks did not represent the official position of the integrated bloc. The condemnation from the parliamentary leadership highlighted the divisions within the Former Detainees’ ranks. The chief whip’s intervention soon triggered a counter-reaction within the group’s leadership. Senior figures, including Dr Majak D’Agoot, Gier Chuang Aluong and Madut Biar Yel, moved to distance themselves from the chief whip’s statement rather than from the vice president. In a subsequent statement, the senior leaders rejected the chief whip’s rebuke, effectively affirming Nyandeng’s right to express her views and aligning themselves with aspects of her criticism of the government. Their response suggests that significant elements of the Former Detainees continue to harbour concerns about the direction of the country and the distribution of political power within the unified SPLM. The fallout from Nyandeng’s remarks, and the subsequent dispute over the chief whip’s intervention, has therefore reopened a critical debate about internal party democracy and the durability of the SPLM’s reunification. It has also placed the Former Detainees at a political crossroads. Political analysts and some party elders argue that, for the sake of South Sudan’s future, the Former Detainees should move beyond the lingering divisions of 2013 and commit themselves fully to working within the unified SPLM under President Salva Kiir Mayardit as its chairman. Unlike the SPLM-IO, which has pursued a separate course as a political rival, the Former Detainees have maintained that their primary objective is to preserve and strengthen the original liberation movement. Continuing to nurture old grievances or perpetuating internal divisions, however, risks weakening the party from within at a time when South Sudan faces significant political, economic and institutional challenges. A sustainable political future requires the Former Detainees to move beyond superficial or transactional power-sharing arrangements and embrace a more coherent role within the party hierarchy. President Kiir, as chairman of the SPLM, represents the institutional continuity of the liberation movement and, in the author’s view, an important anchor of national stability. By consolidating behind his leadership, the Former Detainees could move from being an insulated internal faction to becoming a more effective force within a unified party structure. Only through sustained cooperation under Chairman Kiir, this argument goes, can the SPLM finally move beyond the divisions of 2013, strengthen governance in Juba and lay a more stable foundation for South Sudan’s democratic future. The writer, Amaju Ubur Yalamoi Ayani, is a teacher and political analyst. He can be reached at amajuayani@gmail.com . items.title: South Sudan youth leaders urged to seek political office
items.summary: More than 40 young people from civil society organizations and political parties have taken part The post South Sudan youth leaders urged to seek political office appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: More than 40 young people from civil society organizations and political parties have taken part in a training session in Juba aimed at encouraging greater youth participation in South Sudan’s upcoming elections. The workshop, organized by Markaz al-Salam, focused on moving young people beyond their traditional roles as voters or participants in conflict and encouraging them to seek elected and leadership positions, said Florence Agiba, the organization’s executive director. “What we want this time is not just for youth to be voters, but to be candidates who are voted for,” Agiba said. “We want to see young people in leadership positions across various structures and branches of government, from local councils to the national level.” Agiba said similar programmes had been held in Mundri earlier this year with support from Norwegian People’s Aid (NPA), while another session is tentatively planned for Yambio in October or November. But limited funding is preventing the organization from expanding the programme nationwide, she said. “If we had the resources, visiting the entire country would not be an issue,” Agiba said. She said the organization is also working to ensure implementation of the 20% youth representation quota in decision-making bodies. “We have secured the 20% representation ‘cake’ for young people. Now, it is about teaching them how to claim and share it at the grassroots level, but we are severely constrained by resources,” she said. Agiba expressed concern about declining participation by political party representatives in recent strategy sessions. Of an expected 35 participants drawn from civil society, the private sector and political parties, fewer party representatives attended than at previous workshops, she said. “Those in political parties are key because they are the ones who can implement these reforms internally when they return to their organizations,” she said. “To take up leadership positions, young people need active backing within their parties.” Markaz al-Salam is advocating amendments to the National Elections Act to strengthen youth representation, including urging political parties to establish dedicated youth lists for nominations, Agiba said. The organization is also calling for the mandatory 20% youth representation quota to be implemented across decision-making bodies. Agiba cited a youth representation fact sheet released last year that showed no youth representation in the presidency or national ministries and only two young deputy governors across South Sudan’s 10 states and three administrative areas. “The conversation today is about how we actualize this 20% quota,” Agiba said. “Young people should not only be tools for war, but active tools to build the nation.” South Sudan is due to hold general elections in December, a vote that has been repeatedly delayed since the country gained independence in 2011. items.body: © (DR) Coup de tonnerre dans le landerneau politique camerounais. Dans une lettre datée du 08 septembre 2026 à Yaoundé et publiée il y a quelques minutes sur sa page Facebook certifiée, le Pr Maurice Kamto annonce sa démission des fonctions de président national du MRC. La lettre, d'une page, est adressée au directoire du Mouvement pour la renaissance du Cameroun. "Je vous informe par la présente que dans l'intérêt supérieur de notre parti, de ses nombreux militants et sympathisants, et du Peuple du Changement en général, j'ai décidé de démissionner des fonctions de Président National du Mouvement pour la Renaissance du Cameroun ( MRC ). Cette décision prend effet à compter de ce jour." Le document porte le cachet du parti avec la mention manuscrite "Reçu le 08/09/2026" et une signature. La lettre commence par la formule devenue sa marque de fabrique : "Chers Amis Politiques". Si elle est confirmée, cette démission intervient paradoxalement à un moment où toutes les fédérations réaffirmaient leur fidélité à l'issue de la convention extraordinaire du 21 décembre 2025 qui l'avait ramené à la tête du parti. Dans sa lettre, Kamto invoque "l'intérêt supérieur du parti" sans autre détail sur ses motivations ni sur la suite de son engagement politique. Son premier vice-président, Mamadou Mota , présente aussi sa démission au secrétaire général du parti. Dans sa lettre, il informe de sa démission avec "effet immédiat". Une décision "mûrement réfléchie et dictée exclusivement par l'intérêt supérieur de notre parti face à l'acharnement et à l'oppression qu'exerce le régime à mon endroit", déclare-t-il. Dans l'énoncé des motifs qu'il présente, il refuse d'être "l'instrument" à utiliser pour fragiliser le parti ou bloquer la marche de ce dernier. Il dit priver le régime d'un sujet de focalisation permettant au mouvement de poursuivre ses objectifs. Aucun communiqué officiel du directoire n'a encore été publié. Le MRC s'achemine-t-il vers une transition ou vers une nouvelle crise ? Les prochains développements sur le sujet apporteront plus de précisions. Cet article Cameroun : Maurice Kamto annonce sa démission de la présidence du MRC est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Special Report - Two School Abductions 45 Days Apart. What Happened to Borno's Safe Schools Measures?
items.summary: [Premium Times] Ten days after the abduction of schoolchildren in Mussa, Borno State, Government officials visited Lassa to reassess school security and ordered the implementation of Safe Schools measures in the affected schools. Thirty-five days later, gunmen attacked Government Day Secondary School, Lassa.
items.body:
Ten days after the abduction of schoolchildren in Mussa, Borno State, Government officials visited Lassa to reassess school security and ordered the implementation of Safe Schools measures in the affected schools. Thirty-five days later, gunmen attacked Government Day Secondary School, Lassa.

Ten days after suspected insurgents abducted dozens of children in Mussa , Borno State officials visited neighbouring Lassa to reassess the security situation and evaluate the safety of its public schools.

The delegation, led by the state's Commissioner for Education, Science, Technology and Innovation, Lawan Wakilbe, visited Mussa, Dille and Lassa on 25 May as part of the government's response to the 15 May abduction.

After the assessment, the government said Mr Wakilbe directed that "all Safe School Initiative measures be fully implemented in the affected schools pending further government directives."

Fasuma Askira, education secretary of Askira-Uba Local Government Area, was among the officials listed as members of the delegation.

The government also said the temporary closure and relocation of Government Day Secondary School, Mussa, was an immediate safety measure under the Safe Schools Initiative.

On 29 June, suspected insurgents attacked Government Day Secondary School, Lassa , while students were taking the National Examinations Council examination.

Some abductees were recovered shortly after the attack, but subsequent verification by PREMIUM TIMES established that 36 students and a teacher remained in captivity.

The government had, however, announced Safe Schools measures between the two attacks.

Interviews with parents, community leaders and the local education authority, together with parliamentary and government records reviewed by PREMIUM TIMES, did not establish what measures were implemented at Government Day Secondary School, Lassa, following the May assessment.

Mrs Askira, who was reportedly part of the government delegation that visited Lassa, told PREMIUM TIMES in an interview on 19 August that the Safe Schools programme was not operating in schools in the affected area.

The federal body coordinating the country's Safe Schools response also did not clarify, despite repeated enquiries, whether Mussa or Lassa had been registered, verified or formally assessed under the national programme, what intervention reached the area, or how the Borno government's announced measures related to the federal Safe Schools structure.

The effects of the insecurity have also spread throughout the local education system.

Mrs Askira confirmed that only 56 of Askira-Uba's 113 primary schools were functioning following security-related closures, compared with 76 before the Mussa crisis.

Security concerns around Mussa and Lassa did not begin with the May attack.

More than a year before the Mussa abduction, concerns over the security situation in the communities had reached the House of Representatives.

On 20 February 2024, Midala Balami, who represents Askira-Uba/Hawul Federal Constituency, sponsored a motion titled "Need to Prevent Killings and Deploy Urgent Security Measures in Saban Gari, Kelle, Dille, Lassa and Mussa Towns in Askira-Uba and Hawul Local Government Areas in Borno State."

The House noted that attacks, killings and destruction in the communities had become recurrent and said there was an urgent need for "robust and efficient security measures" to prevent further attacks.

It urged the Nigerian Army and other security agencies to deploy, strengthen and intensify security measures in Mussa, Lassa, Dille and the surrounding axis.

Eight months later, the House again discussed security in the same communities, this time in relation to education.

The House noted that insecurity was affecting students in the communities and called on the Federal Ministry of Education to collaborate with security agencies to ensure the safety of students, teachers and examination materials.

The records show that security concerns in Mussa and Lassa had been formally brought before the National Assembly more than a year before the two school abductions.

PREMIUM TIMES subsequently obtained a register from Mussa Ward councillor Peter Wabba identifying 40 missing children by name, age and family background.

Further checks in the community at the time suggested the number could be higher, with families and local officials producing varying counts.

Mr Wabba later told PREMIUM TIMES that little reliable information about the children's whereabouts had reached grassroots community leaders.

"At our level, there is no information apart from hearsay," he said.

The abduction was followed by visits and other measures by the state government.

Six days later, the delegation led by Mr Wakilbe visited Mussa, Dille and Lassa.

In Mussa, the government announced the temporary closure and relocation of the Government Day Secondary School located there to the Government Secondary School, Uba, describing the decision as an immediate measure under the Safe Schools Initiative.

The government said officials visited the two communities "to reassess the security situation and evaluate safety conditions in public schools within the affected areas."

Eight days after the Borno assessment tour, on 2 June, the House of Representatives again debated school security following the Mussa abduction.

Lawmakers called for intensified efforts to rescue the children and urged enhanced security deployment around vulnerable schools in Borno and elsewhere.

The House also called for improved intelligence gathering, rapid-response mechanisms, surveillance, early-warning systems and community-based security arrangements.

Twenty-seven days later, Government Day Secondary School, Lassa, was attacked.

The Borno Government's May statement says Lassa was visited and its security situation reassessed.

It also says the education commissioner ordered the implementation of Safe Schools measures in affected schools.

Asked during the 19 August interview what education authorities did after Mussa to protect other vulnerable schools, Mrs Askira said the local authority wrote to the ministry and recommended temporary closures in the Mussa and Lassa areas.

Schools on the outskirts and in vulnerable rural communities were temporarily closed, she said, while junior secondary pupils from Mussa were moved to a government boarding school in Uba.

She said discussions were also held with the local government chairman about deploying community vigilantes around schools when classes resumed.

Under the arrangement she described, vigilantes would remain around school premises from the beginning of the school day until closing time.

She also said Mussa and Lassa had some military presence alongside local vigilantes.

But when PREMIUM TIMES asked whether Mussa was covered by the Safe Schools Initiative or another formal school-security programme before the attack, Mrs Askira answered: "No."

After a break in the interview, PREMIUM TIMES returned to the issue.

Mrs Askira initially asked which programme the reporter was referring to.

When the reporter explained that he meant the Safe Schools programme for vulnerable schools, she said:

"We don't have this programme of school initiatives in our schools in that area."

She subsequently said she could not speak for schools in Maiduguri metropolis but expressed doubt that the programme operated in rural local government areas outside the metropolis.

At Mrs Askira's request, PREMIUM TIMES later sent her the principal statements intended for attribution so she could identify any inaccuracies or misquotations.

She corrected the number of functioning primary schools and the spellings of some schools and communities, but retained the substance of her Safe Schools account.

Her account and the government's statement leave a point requiring clarification.

The state government said Mrs Askira was part of a delegation that visited Lassa and that the education commissioner ordered the implementation of Safe Schools measures in affected schools.

Mrs Askira later said the Safe Schools programme was not operating in schools in the area.

The statements do not necessarily conflict. Measures described as part of Safe Schools could have been ordered even where a formal Safe Schools structure was not operating.

But neither the Borno State Government nor the federal Safe Schools coordinating centre has explained what was in place in Askira-Uba.

The Borno government's statement also did not say whether its reference to "Safe School Initiative measures" meant interventions formally coordinated through the National Safe Schools Response Coordination Centre or security arrangements adopted by the state under the wider Safe Schools framework.

PREMIUM TIMES asked the federal coordinating centre to clarify the relationship.

items.title: Sudan: University of Khartoum Counts Cost of Sudan War As 71 Percent of Academics Remain Abroad, Infrastructure Destroyed
items.summary: [Dabanga] Khartoum / Kampala -- More than seven in 10 academics at the University of Khartoum remain outside Sudan, while the war has destroyed or damaged much of the institution's infrastructure, threatening plans for a full return to face-to-face teaching.
items.body:
Khartoum / Kampala — More than seven in 10 academics at the University of Khartoum remain outside Sudan, while the war has destroyed or damaged much of the institution's infrastructure, threatening plans for a full return to face-to-face teaching.

The University of Khartoum has lost more than half of its staff housing and the operational capacity of its lecture halls, laboratories, and hospitals, while more than 90% of its information and communications technology infrastructure has been damaged, according to a new report by the university's Academic Staff Association.

The report, prepared by the association's Committee to Ensure the Continuity of the Educational Process, says a full and immediate return to face-to-face teaching faces major obstacles, including the absence of large numbers of students and academics, fragile infrastructure, and the incomplete rehabilitation of university facilities.

The university administration asked academic staff to return and resume work by 1 August 2026, as part of plans to resume face-to-face teaching for all levels from September and close internal and external teaching and examination centres. However, a survey of 381 staff members found that 71% remained outside Sudan, while 29% were inside the country.

Other data shows that the average number of returning staff in departments at one faculty on the Central Campus was about 20%, while the average in the three best-performing departments at a faculty on the Shambat Campus was about 50%. Attendance at the Education Campus reached 68% by 15 August, compared with only 35% at the Faculty of Arts by 23 August.

The association warns that an inflexible return could lead the university to lose more academic staff and proposes a transitional plan lasting a full academic year.

Among medical students, about 42% are outside Sudan. Only about 54% express confidence in their theoretical knowledge, while more than 75% have major gaps in clinical skills. More than 90% are concerned about clinical training because of shortages of teaching staff and supervisors, and the lack of readiness of medical facilities.

At the Faculty of Engineering, data covering 1,351 students shows that more than 50% are refugees or displaced outside Sudan, while 27% live inside Sudan but outside Khartoum State, meaning that 77.8% are not currently in Khartoum.

The data also shows that 74.7% of engineering students do not have accommodation in Khartoum after examinations end, while 57% say they are either completely unable to afford travel costs or can only afford them with extreme difficulty.

The report warns that closing external examination centres could prevent more than 80% of students from sitting their exams. Student associations have submitted at least 15 memorandums to faculty deans, as well as another to the university's vice-chancellor, without receiving a response.

At the Faculty of Pharmacy, the proportion of admitted students who enrolled was close to 90% before the war, but fell to about 46% for the deferred 2023 intake and 41% for the deferred 2024 intake.

At the Faculty of Education, about 73% of students enrolled, despite the number admitted after the war across two intakes being roughly equivalent to the number previously admitted in a single intake.

Some university assets have sustained damage of up to about 40%, which could be addressed through maintenance and rehabilitation. Damage to other assets exceeds 40%, while some have been damaged so severely that complete replacement would be more appropriate.

The Faculty of Science has lost about 12 laboratories, including around seven that have been completely destroyed. The Faculty of Pharmacy and the main examination hall have also sustained severe damage, alongside near-total losses of vehicles, furniture, computers, servers, network systems, and digital assets.

Despite the destruction, the university continued online teaching during the war, held six examination sessions, and graduated about 8,000 students. A seventh session was later held in person at university premises in Khartoum, but saw a noticeable absence among students registered to sit the exams.

Before the war, the university's Academic Council approved a system allowing 50% online teaching to address the accumulation of student cohorts.

As part of rehabilitation efforts, the estimated cost of repairing the Baghdad Hall at the Faculty of Medicine is about $130,000, while repairs to the Anis Hall are estimated at about 300m Sudanese pounds. Rehabilitation work has also been carried out at the Faculty of Engineering and several other faculties, with support from graduates and the private sector.

The committee proposes a phased participation system for academics over one academic year, divided into three categories: full return, hybrid participation, and remote online work.

Under the proposal, academics in the hybrid category would spend between four and six weeks on campus during each semester, while carrying out the remainder of their duties remotely. The university would cover one return air ticket per semester and provide living expenses during their stay.

The committee also recommends reopening external centres for a full academic year, adopting blended learning over the same period, and automatically renewing monthly contracts during the transitional year.

Those unable to return after the end of the academic year would be allowed to apply for statutory leave in accordance with university regulations.

The committee calls for a specialist academic committee on blended learning, as well as a higher committee for rebuilding the university, involving academics, students, and graduates.

It also calls for a reconstruction strategy aimed not simply at restoring the university to its pre-war condition, but rebuilding it according to a new vision.

The University of Khartoum, whose history dates back to 1902, had about 44,000 undergraduate and intermediate diploma students in 2025, as well as about 10,000 postgraduate students.

It employed 5,501 staff, of whom academics accounted for 36% and non-academic employees 64%.

The university includes 23 faculties, 12 research institutes, 10 research centres, four university hospitals, and five main campuses. Its housing facilities previously accommodated more than 20% of academic staff and senior employees, while it was linked to about 1,395 cooperating institutions through academic and research partnerships and agreements.

items.title: UN Human Rights Council Urged to Widen Sudan Arms Embargo and Extend Fact-Finding Mission
items.summary: [Dabanga] Geneva / Amsterdam -- The UN's Sudan fact-finding mission has urged the Human Rights Council to expand the Darfur arms embargo to the whole country, warning that foreign support is sustaining a war in which both sides may have committed war crimes. Sudan's government, however, rejects efforts to treat the warring parties as equivalent and says the conflict is being prolonged by external
items.body:
Geneva / Amsterdam — The UN's Sudan fact-finding mission has urged the Human Rights Council to expand the Darfur arms embargo to the whole country, warning that foreign support is sustaining a war in which both sides may have committed war crimes. Sudan's government, however, rejects efforts to treat the warring parties as equivalent and says the conflict is being prolonged by external backing for the Rapid Support Forces.

Many of the violations documented in Sudan may amount to international crimes, and responsibility could extend to those who finance, supply, or otherwise enable them, Mohamed Chande Othman, chair of the UN Fact-Finding Mission on Sudan, told the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council at the Palais des Nations in Geneva, Switzerland on Monday.

He said drones had reshaped the battlefield, fuelled by external support in the form of weapons, logistics, and personnel, while the growing use of long-range drones had had devastating consequences for civilians and essential services.

The mission is continuing its investigation into attacks in El Obeid, which have forced civilians to flee, as well as attacks on Kadugli, Ed Daein, and Yabus.

Othman said both sides had committed violations that may amount to war crimes. He described a cross-border network facilitating military operations involving the United Arab Emirates, Chad, Libya, which he said had supplied weapons to Nyala.

Colombians had also been recruited into the Rapid Support Forces to operate drones and provide training, he said, adding that the mission's investigation into external support for the Sudanese Armed Forces was continuing.

Othman said states had a responsibility not only to refrain from violations, but also to take reasonable measures to prevent them where there was a clear and foreseeable risk.

Survivors, witnesses, journalists, lawyers, and human rights defenders face intimidation and harassment from all parties to the conflict, both inside and outside Sudan, particularly because of their cooperation with investigative missions, he said.

He called for an end to reprisals and said the international community had a responsibility to act rather than merely document violations.

The mission recommended an immediate end to the war, full compliance with international human rights and humanitarian law, and all possible precautions to protect civilians and civilian objects.

It called for unlawful military support to be halted, and urged states to investigate individuals and entities under their jurisdiction that provide such support. It also called for the Darfur arms embargo to be enforced and expanded across Sudan , echoing proposals before the UN Security Council.

The mission urged the preservation of evidence, protection for victims and witnesses, and effective assistance and remedies for survivors, while calling for accountability across the full chain of responsibility, including those who commit, order, finance, supply, or facilitate international crimes.

Sudan's attorney general and head of the National Committee for the Investigation of Crimes and Violations of National and International Humanitarian Law, Intisar Abdel Aal, presented a sharply different account of the conflict.

She described the war as a "proxy war", citing multiple international reports, and directly accused the United Arab Emirates of being the "sponsor of the rebel militia", saying its external support for the Rapid Support Forces was the main reason the war had been prolonged and atrocities committed.

She called for the UAE to be condemned and for decisive action to stop its support, but rejected calls to expand the arms embargo, describing them as the adoption of demands made by the "rebel militia".

Abdel Aal also pointed to the work of Sudan's national investigation committee, saying it had made significant progress as the Sudanese Armed Forces advanced and security was restored.

The attorney general announced the launch of a Sudanese-Sudanese dialogue for peace, declared by the chair of the Transitional Sovereignty Council, and said participants would be provided with guarantees and immunities.

The Arab League and African Union had welcomed the dialogue, she said, adding that justice and peace were complementary.

The National Committee for Investigation has documented 153,112 criminal cases in accordance with national and international standards.

Immunity was lifted in 391 cases involving members of regular forces, while 6,862 cases were withdrawn during the investigation stage. Investigations were completed in 22,608 cases and referred to national courts, which ruled on 10,733 cases.

The attorney general said the committee had documented 2,261 cases of rape against women and girls, 15,227 cases of detention and enforced disappearance, 32,622 deaths, and 443 injuries.

She called on the council and UN mechanisms to follow the principle of complementarity rather than imposing external mechanisms.

The European Union called for all states and external actors to stop actions and support that fuel the conflict, and backed the renewal of the Fact-Finding Mission's mandate to allow it to continue collecting and preserving evidence.

The eight Nordic and Baltic countries also called for the mandate to be renewed and for the mission to be granted access to Sudan, stressing its role in documenting violations, preserving evidence, and laying the foundations for accountability.

Their statement said external support was helping sustain military operations and strengthening the capacities of the warring parties. It urged all states to halt funding and support enabling the conflict, and called on the parties to agree to a sustainable ceasefire, protect civilians and humanitarian workers, and ensure safe and unhindered humanitarian access.

Luxembourg expressed deep concern about drone attacks on civilians and protected infrastructure, calling for full respect for the Darfur arms embargo and stronger mechanisms to track arms transfers.

Together, the European Union, Nordic and Baltic countries, and Luxembourg backed continued international scrutiny and measures aimed at preserving evidence, strengthening accountability, and preventing further violations.

Kenya's representative, speaking on behalf of the African Group, emphasised a third strand of the debate, stressing the need to respect Sudan's sovereignty, unity, and independence, and calling for African solutions to African problems.

The representative called for efforts to be coordinated under the auspices of the African Union and Arab League, condemned interference in Sudan's internal affairs that fuels the conflict, and stressed the need to continue dialogue towards democratic transition.

The statement welcomed the Sudanese government's cooperation with relevant actors and said the state bore the primary responsibility for promoting human rights.

Egypt's representative went further in rejecting the equivalence drawn by some international assessments between the warring parties. He said Sudanese people continued to pay the price for violations committed by the Rapid Support Forces, rejected any attempt to equate the army with the RSF, and opposed interference in Sudan's affairs and threats to its unity.

DefendDefenders described the Fact-Finding Mission as indispensable and said the conduct of the warring parties showed a complete disregard for international law and their obligations under the Jeddah Declaration.

It said about 70 civil society organisations had called for the mission's mandate to be extended in full for two years, with sufficient resources and expertise to continue documenting violations, investigating alleged crimes, and preserving evidence.

The organisation called for the mission's findings, including its urgent investigation into El Obeid, to feed into wider accountability efforts by the Human Rights Council and the UN system.

It also urged the international community to give greater priority to Sudan, saying the UN General Assembly could submit the mission's reports to the Security Council, while actors with influence over the warring parties should address the role of external forces in sustaining the conflict and enabling atrocities.

items.title: UN calls for immediate ceasefire as Sudan crisis deepens
items.summary: The United Nations is calling for an immediate ceasefire in Sudan, as drone attacks and the destruction of healthcare facilities deepen an already devastating humanitarian crisis.
items.body:
The United Nations is calling for an immediate ceasefire in Sudan, as drone attacks and the destruction of healthcare facilities deepen an already devastating humanitarian crisis.

More than six million people have been displaced inside Sudan, while another 4.5 million have fled the country.

UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk says civilians in several regions face an imminent risk of further attacks, calling for an end to foreign involvement and a return to civilian rule.

UN investigators say both the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces are increasingly using long-range drones, extending attacks far beyond traditional front lines.

In South Kordofan, strikes on a kindergarten and hospital killed 114 people, including 60 children.

A separate attack on a teaching hospital killed at least 70 people.

Investigators say there are reasonable grounds to believe both sides committed serious violations that may amount to war crimes.

items.summary: Residents of Al-Mudayib village in Sudan’s North Darfur State have appealed to the relevant authorities The post Residents of North Darfur village urge reopening of school closed since war began appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: Residents of Al-Mudayib village in Sudan’s North Darfur State have appealed to the relevant authorities to reopen the area’s only school, which has been closed since the war began in April 2023. Ibrahim Ahmed Al-Doudo, chairperson of the school’s education council, told Radio Tamazuj on Tuesday that the school had not reopened since fighting broke out. Three of its six classrooms need to be rebuilt, while accommodation for teachers also needs to be constructed, he said. The school had 654 pupils, both boys and girls, before the war, Al-Doudo said. They have now been out of school for more than three years. Several university graduates from the area have offered to volunteer as teachers if the school reopens, he said. The school also lacks desks, textbooks and other educational materials, while funds are needed to support volunteer teachers, Al-Doudo said. Tribo Burma Yousif, a resident of Al-Mudayib, said the closure had severely affected the community and urged authorities, donors and other well-wishers to help restore the school. He said traditional Quranic schools in the area had also been forced to close or damaged because of the conflict. Al-Mudayib School, established in 1994, was originally known as Al-Mudayib Mixed Basic School and had eight classrooms. Its capacity was later reduced to six classrooms following Sudan’s education reforms, which introduced a six-year primary cycle followed by three years each of intermediate and secondary education. The school is in the Mustariha administrative unit of Al-Waha locality in North Darfur state. Mustariha was the stronghold of tribal leader Musa Hilal, who had declared his support for the Sudanese army. The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) attacked the area in February, taking control after fighting with forces aligned with Hilal and prompting the displacement of thousands of residents. The conflict between Sudan’s army and the RSF began in April 2023 and has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions, according to the United Nations and aid agencies. The war has also severely disrupted education, with schools destroyed, damaged or used for other purposes and millions of children deprived of regular schooling. The post Residents of North Darfur village urge reopening of school closed since war began appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

items.title: South Darfur: University of Nyala prepares to resume in-person classes
items.summary: A campaign to rehabilitate the University of Nyala has begun in the capital of Sudan’s The post South Darfur: University of Nyala prepares to resume in-person classes appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: A campaign to rehabilitate the University of Nyala has begun in the capital of Sudan’s South Darfur state, as authorities prepare to resume in-person classes after years of disruption caused by the war. The work includes repairing and refurbishing classrooms, faculty buildings and administrative offices, officials overseeing the campaign said. Mohamed Hassan Al-Taayshi, prime minister of the Tasees government, visited the university to inspect the rehabilitation work and review its progress. The Tasees government, an RSF-aligned administration known as the Government of Peace and Unity, is headquartered in Nyala. Al-Taayshi said universities in areas controlled by the Tasees government had sufficient capacity to accommodate students. Where capacity was insufficient, authorities would resort to online education using internet services. The prime minister also praised residents for protecting the University of Nyala from destruction and vandalism during the war. Al-Noor Ali Ahmed Fadl, head of the popular committee overseeing the campaign, thanked Al-Taayshi for his support, saying it had helped overcome obstacles facing the rehabilitation effort. Higher Education Minister Eid Ibrahim Breima said classes would initially resume in person before later shifting to online learning. He said the government planned in the next phase to share the cost of higher education with the public, with greater emphasis on applied fields such as engineering, medicine and agriculture to help develop a skilled workforce. Sudan’s war erupted on April 15, 2023, when fighting broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict has displaced more than 14 million people, according to the United Nations. The RSF controls most of Darfur, including Nyala, while the army holds large areas of eastern and central Sudan. Millions of Sudanese have fled their homes, with many crossing into neighbouring countries including Chad, Egypt and South Sudan. The post South Darfur: University of Nyala prepares to resume in-person classes appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

items.title: Leaked files shed new light on Sudan Army’s alleged chemical weapons program
items.summary: The SAF has found itself at the center of a major crisis following news investigations by leading U.S. media outlets that exposed its involvement in developing and deploying chemical weapons. The post Leaked files shed new light on Sudan Army’s alleged chemical weapons program appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have found themselves at the center of a major crisis following news investigations by leading U.S. media outlets that exposed their involvement in developing and deploying chemical weapons in the ongoing conflict against the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Mohsin Osman reports. On Saturday, The New York Times and The Washington Post published dual investigative reports based on leaked intelligence materials. The files include approximately 150 documents, photographs, video clips, and intercepted communications, alongside thousands of text messages retrieved from the phones of Sudanese officers. The evidence points to an alleged program established in 2024 to manufacture chlorine-based munitions. It details bomb design blueprints, testing operations, and a coordinated cover-up strategy initiated after the plot was uncovered by the United States. The records also outline plans to siphon chlorine gas from a civilian water treatment facility that had originally received the chemical from international aid agencies. These revelations reignite long-standing allegations of chemical weapons usage that have shadowed SAF leadership since last year, significantly heightening international pressure on the military command. The United States previously imposed sanctions on Sudan in May 2025 over allegations that the military deployed chemical weapons during the conflict in 2024. The sanctions took effect on July 20, 2025. Authorities in Port Sudan have consistently rejected these accusations, maintaining that they do not produce, stockpile, or use chemical weapons, and emphasizing their adherence to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC). A Covert Program Amid Escalating Pressure According to The New York Times, the SAF turned to chemical weapons early in 2024 to break a strategic stalemate, as RSF fighters held firm control over most of the capital, Khartoum. Leaked records show that Brigadier General Tariq Hussein emerged as a central figure in July 2024, orchestrating the design, planning, and execution of the program. Intercepted messages reveal that Hussein proposed using chlorine to give army forces a tactical edge in the battle for Khartoum. He distributed prototype schematics for an explosive warhead integrated with roughly 33 pounds of chlorine gas, with production commencing that same month. In messages published by the Times, Hussein noted that the hybrid munitions were designed to maximize lethality—either by shrapnel fragmentation or chlorine gas poisoning—asserting that the explosion would destroy all chemical traces of the attack. On July 22, an Antonov cargo plane took off from Merowe Airport, roughly 200 miles north of Khartoum, to conduct a test launch. Following the trial, Hussein reported that the experiment was a “100 percent success,” attaching a video of a desert explosion and confirming that the munition “hit the target and released the gas.” Brigadier General Amir Idris, identified in records as the supervisor of military drone operations, responded with a single directive: “Top Secret.” Technical Hazards and Signs of Lethality The communications reveal that the program faced severe technical flaws. Chemical leaks were a recurring issue; on one occasion, workers found dead insects and scorpions on the floor of a hangar after overnight exposure to leaking gas. The incident underscored the volatile nature of the agent being handled long before it reached the battlefield. Concurrently, the program faced a critical challenge in securing a steady supply of chlorine. Diverting Humanitarian Chlorine Supplies According to The New York Times, 20 cylinders of chlorine gas were smuggled across the border from a neighboring country in late August 2024. Hussein calculated that this batch would yield roughly 1,100 bombs. Hussein subsequently sought internal sources, turning to local civilian infrastructure in violation of international norms. He admitted to sourcing additional chlorine from the Al-Manara water treatment plant in Omdurman—one of the few remaining operational facilities amid the war. “Al-Manara has some of those cylinders, and we took them from there,” Hussein stated in an August 26 voice message to Idris. The diversion of these supplies carries significant gravity, as the chlorine at the plant was intended for emergency water purification during cholera outbreaks rather than military application. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) confirmed to the Times that it had donated 30 chlorine cylinders to the plant in 2023, while CARE reported delivering 35 cylinders across 2024 and 2025. A UNICEF spokesperson added that the organization supplied chlorine to six treatment plants in Khartoum, including Al-Manara, between 2023 and 2025. By October 2024, Hussein reported manufacturing approximately 300 chemical munitions, most of which were stored at Merowe Airport. Earlier in September, Hussein sent a notable message to a colleague stating, “They drank the gas,” describing an attack on RSF fighters at the Al-Jaili oil refinery north of Khartoum. This account aligns with claims made by the RSF on September 13, when the paramilitary group issued a statement accusing the army of firing “toxic” missiles at the refinery. Footage circulated online at the time showed men in civilian clothing inside the facility wearing oxygen masks. Command Responsibility and Cover-Up Efforts The New York Times indicates that the program was likely shuttered once U.S. officials detected its existence and moved to apply targeted sanctions. Intercepted communications reveal that the head of Sudan’s Armed Forces, General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, instructed Hussein to “erase all traces” of the operation. The response was: “The operation was completed a month ago.” During a subsequent round of measures in June, the U.S. sanctioned Hussein for importing explosives for bomb production, though that specific designation did not explicitly cite chemical weapons. By that time, Burhan had established an internal committee to investigate the U.S. allegations. According to documents in the file, Hussein himself—the architect of the program—was appointed as an advisor to the panel. The intelligence indicates that General Burhan was not merely informed after the fact, but was directly involved in overseeing the chemical weapons program. His direct knowledge was a primary factor in the U.S. decision to impose sanctions on him in January 2025. While proving chemical weapons usage in conflict zones remains complex, arms experts consulted by The New York Times concurred that available evidence strongly points to their deployment in the Sudanese conflict. However, they stressed the necessity of an independent field investigation. Addressing the findings, the Emergency Lawyers group, a Sudanese legal advocacy organization, issued a statement calling for a transparent international probe. The group urged that “international experts be granted safe, unconditional access to targeted sites, enable the physical examination of munitions fragments and delivery systems, and be permitted to interview witnesses and victims independently and securely.” The post Leaked files shed new light on Sudan Army’s alleged chemical weapons program appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

items.title: ‘We have not gone missing’: Machar lawyer
items.summary: A lawyer defending suspended South Sudanese First Vice President Riek Machar on Tuesday denied social The post ‘We have not gone missing’: Machar lawyer appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: A lawyer defending suspended South Sudanese First Vice President Riek Machar on Tuesday denied social media reports that he and the lead defence counsel had gone missing in Juba after allegedly being arrested by the National Security Service. Kur Lual Kur, a member of Machar’s defence team, told Radio Tamazuj on Tuesday that the reports that he and lead defense lawyer Geri Raimondo Legge were missing were false. “What is being circulated on social media that we are missing is not true, so we would like to refute that,” Kur said. Kur said, however, that the defence team had received threats and would present details to the special court when Machar’s trial resumes on Friday. “Yes, there are threats, but we will present it before the court on Friday. During Friday’s session we will clarify and explain the challenges and risks facing us,” he said. “We are fine and we have not gone missing,” he said. The defence team raised concerns about alleged threats against its eight clients and members of the legal team during Monday’s proceedings. Legge told the court that there was a “serious threat” to the defence team and the eight accused, particularly Machar, and called for the matter to be addressed urgently. He did not identify those allegedly responsible. The court adjourned proceedings on Monday after one of the three judges, Stephen Simon, was unable to attend because he was unwell. The trial is due to resume on Friday. Machar and seven co-defendants are being tried over violence in Nasir, Upper Nile state, in March 2025. They face charges including treason, murder, conspiracy, terrorism, destruction of public property and crimes against humanity. Prosecutors allege that forces loyal to Machar, together with the White Army militia, killed 257 government soldiers during an attack on a military garrison in Nasir. The post ‘We have not gone missing’: Machar lawyer appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

items.title: Aviation civile : le Cameroun abrite l’atelier africain sur la préparation aux urgences sanitaires

L'École de Formation de la CCAA à Nsimalen abrite la 12ème réunion du CAPSCA Afrique et l'atelier sur la préparation aux urgences de santé publique en aviation, réunissant les délégués du Cameroun et de tout le continent. C'est un rendez-vous stratégique pour l'avenir du transport aérien africa
items.body: © DR Du 7 au 11 septembre 2026, Yaoundé devient la capitale africaine de la sécurité sanitaire aérienne. L'École de Formation de la CCAA à Nsimalen abrite la 12ème réunion du CAPSCA Afrique et l'atelier sur la préparation aux urgences de santé publique en aviation, réunissant les délégués du Cameroun et de tout le continent. C'est un rendez-vous stratégique pour l'avenir du transport aérien africain. Pendant cinq jours, les experts du programme CAPSCA (Collaborative Arrangement for the Prevention and Management of Public Health Events in Civil Aviation) vont plancher sur les spécificités de chaque État et les difficultés rencontrées sur le terrain. L'objectif est clair : tirer les leçons des crises passées, notamment le Covid-19, pour mieux prévenir et gérer les futures urgences de santé publique susceptibles de paralyser l'aviation civile. Pour le Cameroun, pays hôte, cette rencontre est une reconnaissance. Yaoundé a déjà engagé des actions significatives qui font office de modèle : renforcement de la coordination entre les secteurs de l'aviation et de la santé, élaboration de plans d'urgence sanitaire pour les aéroports internationaux de Douala et Yaoundé-Nsimalen, et réalisation d'audits de supervision sanitaire. Au-delà de l'aspect technique, cet atelier traduit l'engagement du Cameroun en faveur de ses obligations internationales en matière de sûreté et de résilience de l'aviation civile. En accueillant l'Afrique à Nsimalen, le pays affirme sa volonté de jouer un rôle moteur dans la construction d'un ciel africain plus sûr face aux menaces sanitaires. Cet article Aviation civile : le Cameroun abrite l’atelier africain sur la préparation aux urgences sanitaires est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Elections: UJOSS brings together media, security, and civil society in Yei
items.summary: At least 25 stakeholders, including 12 journalists, security officials, members of civil society and electoral The post Elections: UJOSS brings together media, security, and civil society in Yei appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: At least 25 stakeholders, including 12 journalists, security officials, members of civil society and electoral officials in Central Equatoria State’s Yei River County, have called for stronger cooperation to promote peaceful elections and responsible use of digital platforms. The call was made on Monday during a stakeholders’ engagement meeting organized by the Union of Journalists of South Sudan (UJOSS) Central Equatoria State Branch, with support from Norwegian People’s Aid (NPA) at the Yei Resource Center. Speaking during the closing of the meeting, Buga Alex, the Central Equatoria Coordinator for the UJOSS branch in Yei, called for the protection of press freedom, emphasizing the important role of every actor before, during, and after the elections. “Anyone cannot do this if journalists are threatened, beaten, or if our equipment is confiscated. Therefore, I call upon all actors to protect press freedom. Civil society organizations are the bridge between government and the people, and have a great responsibility in civic education,” he said. “The organized forces, our brothers and sisters in uniform, your role is very important, and it is not politics but protection. You have to protect us, the voters, the ballot boxes, the journalists, and electoral officials.” “When the process is professional and neutral, people will trust the electoral process and come out to vote in big numbers,” Buga added. Modi Arkangelo, Chairperson of Civil Society in Greater Yei, called for stronger collaboration between state authorities and the media, particularly in providing accurate information to the public. “The media becomes the fourth pillar or organ of the government. A country without the media is a dead country because there is no information flow,” he said. “The media falls within the jurisdiction of civil society when people are preparing for elections. All the hopes are looking forward to seeing what role we can play to educate the people to know what they can do.” On his part, Clement Benet, Director for Youth, Culture and Sports in Yei River County, urged the public to protect their personal data against cyberattacks and hacking and further encouraged social media users to use their real names and share accurate information to make it easier to recover their accounts in case they are lost or compromised. “What is very important to us is that when you want to open an account, you should use your real name because that becomes easy to track, especially when your information gets lost, and be cautious with hacking or cybercrime,” he counselled. Meanwhile, Dominic Wawa, a participant in the panel discussion, described the session as productive, saying it has helped prepare stakeholders for the forthcoming elections while also increasing their knowledge of cybercrime and cybersecurity. “We discussed vital information regarding our preparation and readiness for the forthcoming election that is ahead of us. We are left with only 109 days to the election; that means that there is a lot that we need to do,” he said. “I learned a lot; cybersecurity and computer misuse mean a lot to us. This information needs to go out there so that we do not become victims.” Jennifer Nyoka, a female participant, called for greater caution in dealing with cybercrime and issues surrounding the upcoming elections. “I will be going back home with something important regarding the election,” she said. “I learned mostly about cybercrime, and we should be vigilant and very careful about things concerning the internet, fraud, hackers, and misuse of identity because someone might use another’s account illegally.” The session provided an opportunity to raise awareness about cybercrime, responsible use of computers and digital platforms, and the need for citizens and media practitioners to understand the legal implications of misusing digital technologies, including provisions under the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act. The post Elections: UJOSS brings together media, security, and civil society in Yei appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

items.title: As Justin Davis Leaves Mogadishu, Washington Is Asking a Different Question About Somalia
items.summary: As Justin Davis concludes his tenure as Chargé d’Affaires at the United States Embassy in Mogadishu, he leaves at a time when the relationship between Somalia and the U.S.is changing, perhaps more significantly than official statements suggest. Over recent months, I have spoken with several American diplomats in Mogadishu, Nairobi, New York, Washington and elsewhere […] The post As Justin Davis Le
items.body: As Justin Davis concludes his tenure as Chargé d’Affaires at the United States Embassy in Mogadishu, he leaves at a time when the relationship between Somalia and the U.S.is changing, perhaps more significantly than official statements suggest. Over recent months, I have spoken with several American diplomats in Mogadishu, Nairobi, New York, Washington and elsewhere about where the U.S. now stands on Somalia. Some are serving officials, while others know the Somalia file closely. They did not agree on everything and some were more candid than others, but the conversations repeatedly came back to the same question: how much responsibility are Somalis themselves prepared to take for the future of their country? Davis has run the US Embassy through a particularly difficult period. Politics in Washington changed sharply as “America First” came to define the administration’s approach abroad. In Somalia, political divisions deepened, relations between the Federal Government and some Federal Member States deteriorated and Al-Shabaab and Daesh continued to pose serious security threats. At the same time, competition among foreign powers for influence in Somalia and the wider Horn of Africa intensified. One American diplomat described Davis’s challenge to me as finding a way to reconcile “America First” with “Somalia First”. When I asked what “Somalia First” meant, the answer was strikingly straightforward: Somalia for Somalis, strong Somali institutions and political leaders taking responsibility for their own country. Several diplomats worried that foreign interests had become too entangled with Somalia’s domestic political competition and that Somali politicians were themselves sometimes opening the door to that interference. “Somalia’s future is not for sale,” one diplomat told me. It was not an argument for Somalia to turn away from international partners. The country needs them and none of the Americans I spoke with disputed that. Their concern was that Somalia cannot insist on its sovereignty while allowing domestic political disputes to become entangled with competing foreign agendas. In their view, Somali politicians have to find ways of settling their differences without constantly looking towards foreign capitals. Another diplomat was equally direct. “Somalia is not a child. Somalia is a partner,” he said. America was prepared to cooperate with Somalia and support it, but the relationship had to be one between partners, with Somalia taking responsibility for its own choices and future. Under the current US policy, American interests in Somalia have become narrower and more clearly defined. Three priorities came up repeatedly in my conversations: counterterrorism, law enforcement cooperation and immigration coordination. These are increasingly the hard interests around which Washington is organising its relationship with Mogadishu. But the American assessment of Somalia was far from entirely negative. Diplomats acknowledged good progress in law enforcement cooperation and immigration coordination and spoke positively about the working relationship with Somali authorities in these areas. They also recognised that Mogadishu is considerably more peaceful than it was before, something several of them regarded as an important achievement that should not be overlooked. Their frustration was much greater when the conversation moved beyond Mogadishu. American diplomats were unhappy with the pace of counter-offensive operations against Al-Shabaab outside the capital. They had expected greater movement and more sustained gains on the ground. Their concern was not simply about launching military operations but whether those operations were producing lasting results and maintaining sufficient pressure on Al-Shabaab. Politics inevitably entered that discussion. Several diplomats believed the prolonged confrontation between the federal government, federal member states and opposition politicians was taking attention away from the security campaign. To them, political cohesion and the fight against Al-Shabaab are not separate issues. A country whose political leaders are consumed by disputes among themselves will inevitably find it more difficult to sustain a coherent national security effort. The reduction in American humanitarian and development assistance also reflects the wider change in Washington. One diplomat pushed back when I described this as a retreat from humanitarian engagement. He preferred to call it a “reorganisation of assistance”, with more emphasis on priorities, accountability and results. Others were more candid in acknowledging that America’s broader interest in Somalia had declined and that Washington was reconsidering how much money and political attention it was prepared to commit. Some also admitted that Washington itself had spent several years struggling to decide exactly what its overriding national security interests in Somalia were. Over time, American engagement had expanded into counterterrorism, security assistance, humanitarian relief, state-building, democratisation and political mediation. The current approach is much less expansive. The message now is simpler: America will help Somalia, but Somalia must also help itself. That view becomes particularly clear when American diplomats talk about Somali politics. They see fragmentation on almost every side. Within the federal government, the executive, parliament and other state institutions appear increasingly aligned. Yet relations between Mogadishu and important Federal Member States remain badly fractured, particularly with Puntland and Jubaland. The Americans are not putting all the blame on Villa Somalia. They are also critical of the opposition. Several diplomats, in separate conversations, used exactly the same word to describe it: “fragmented”. They questioned how much opposition leaders trust one another and whether their alliances are built around a common political programme or simply the convenience of opposing the current leadership. One diplomat posed a difficult question: if opposition to one administration is what brings everyone together, what happens when that administration is no longer there? What struck me during these conversations was that the Americans were rarely questioning the competence of Somalis themselves. They spoke about capable politicians, professionals, entrepreneurs, civil society leaders and a remarkably resilient population. Their frustration was that all this talent had still not produced enough political cohesion around a minimum national interest. One senior diplomat used the U.S. itself as an example. He spoke about “American exceptionalism”, not to suggest that American politicians agree with one another, but almost to make the opposite point. American politics can be bitterly divided, he said, yet there remains a sense of national identity and certain interests around which Americans can still rally. His question was: what is the Somali equivalent? Curiously, the Americans saw a glimpse of an answer in the controversy involving Somalia’s renowned referee Omar Artan. A senior diplomat told me that when Artan was returned from the U.S. and was not allowed into the country, calls to the US Embassy in Mogadishu were incessant. According to the diplomat, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud was among those seeking an explanation. But what fascinated American officials even more was the public reaction that followed. Diplomats in Washington, Mogadishu, Nairobi and elsewhere were closely watching the scenes of large numbers of young Somalis gathering at Mogadishu Stadium. They saw Somalis who would normally find themselves on different sides of political divides rallying around the same issue. It prompted a question among some of those watching: if Somalis could rally together so powerfully around Omar Artan, why could that same sense of national solidarity not be mobilised around Somalia? For some of the diplomats, the episode demonstrated that the national feeling exists. The problem is turning it into a political culture that can survive elections, clan calculations, disputes between governments and the influence of foreign powers. There is an obvious contradiction in some of this American thinking and the diplomats themselves are not unaware of it. For years, the U.S. was one of the most influential external actors in Somali politics. When a serious political crisis erupted, Somali leaders and international partners looked towards Washington. The Americans convened, persuaded, applied pressure and helped push political rivals towards compromise. That America is less visible today. Some Somali politicians and international partners regard this as a weakness in the current American approach. They believe Washington has withdrawn too far from political engagement and that its reduced role has left a vacuum at precisely the wrong time. items.title: University of Khartoum counts cost of Sudan war as 71% of academics remain abroad, infrastructure destroyed
items.summary: More than seven in 10 academics at the University of Khartoum remain outside Sudan, while... The post University of Khartoum counts cost of Sudan war as 71% of academics remain abroad, infrastructure destroyed appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .
items.body: More than seven in 10 academics at the University of Khartoum remain outside Sudan, while the war has destroyed or damaged much of the institution’s infrastructure, threatening plans for a full return to face-to-face teaching. The University of Khartoum has lost more than half of its staff housing and the operational capacity of its lecture halls, laboratories, and hospitals, while more than 90% of its information and communications technology infrastructure has been damaged, according to a new report by the university’s Academic Staff Association. The report, prepared by the association’s Committee to Ensure the Continuity of the Educational Process, says a full and immediate return to face-to-face teaching faces major obstacles, including the absence of large numbers of students and academics, fragile infrastructure, and the incomplete rehabilitation of university facilities. The university administration asked academic staff to return and resume work by 1 August 2026, as part of plans to resume face-to-face teaching for all levels from September and close internal and external teaching and examination centres. However, a survey of 381 staff members found that 71% remained outside Sudan, while 29% were inside the country. Other data shows that the average number of returning staff in departments at one faculty on the Central Campus was about 20%, while the average in the three best-performing departments at a faculty on the Shambat Campus was about 50%. Attendance at the Education Campus reached 68% by 15 August, compared with only 35% at the Faculty of Arts by 23 August. A transitional plan for a full academic year The association warns that an inflexible return could lead the university to lose more academic staff and proposes a transitional plan lasting a full academic year. Among medical students, about 42% are outside Sudan. Only about 54% express confidence in their theoretical knowledge, while more than 75% have major gaps in clinical skills. More than 90% are concerned about clinical training because of shortages of teaching staff and supervisors, and the lack of readiness of medical facilities. At the Faculty of Engineering, data covering 1,351 students shows that more than 50% are refugees or displaced outside Sudan, while 27% live inside Sudan but outside Khartoum State, meaning that 77.8% are not currently in Khartoum. The data also shows that 74.7% of engineering students do not have accommodation in Khartoum after examinations end, while 57% say they are either completely unable to afford travel costs or can only afford them with extreme difficulty. The report warns that closing external examination centres could prevent more than 80% of students from sitting their exams. Student associations have submitted at least 15 memorandums to faculty deans, as well as another to the university’s vice-chancellor, without receiving a response. At the Faculty of Pharmacy, the proportion of admitted students who enrolled was close to 90% before the war, but fell to about 46% for the deferred 2023 intake and 41% for the deferred 2024 intake. At the Faculty of Education, about 73% of students enrolled, despite the number admitted after the war across two intakes being roughly equivalent to the number previously admitted in a single intake. Laboratories completely destroyed Some university assets have sustained damage of up to about 40%, which could be addressed through maintenance and rehabilitation. Damage to other assets exceeds 40%, while some have been damaged so severely that complete replacement would be more appropriate. The Faculty of Science has lost about 12 laboratories, including around seven that have been completely destroyed. The Faculty of Pharmacy and the main examination hall have also sustained severe damage, alongside near-total losses of vehicles, furniture, computers, servers, network systems, and digital assets. Despite the destruction, the university continued online teaching during the war, held six examination sessions, and graduated about 8,000 students. A seventh session was later held in person at university premises in Khartoum, but saw a noticeable absence among students registered to sit the exams. Before the war, the university’s Academic Council approved a system allowing 50% online teaching to address the accumulation of student cohorts. Phased system for academics As part of rehabilitation efforts, the estimated cost of repairing the Baghdad Hall at the Faculty of Medicine is about $130,000, while repairs to the Anis Hall are estimated at about 300m Sudanese pounds. Rehabilitation work has also been carried out at the Faculty of Engineering and several other faculties, with support from graduates and the private sector. The committee proposes a phased participation system for academics over one academic year, divided into three categories: full return, hybrid participation, and remote online work. Under the proposal, academics in the hybrid category would spend between four and six weeks on campus during each semester, while carrying out the remainder of their duties remotely. The university would cover one return air ticket per semester and provide living expenses during their stay. The committee also recommends reopening external centres for a full academic year, adopting blended learning over the same period, and automatically renewing monthly contracts during the transitional year. Those unable to return after the end of the academic year would be allowed to apply for statutory leave in accordance with university regulations. The committee calls for a specialist academic committee on blended learning, as well as a higher committee for rebuilding the university, involving academics, students, and graduates. It also calls for a reconstruction strategy aimed not simply at restoring the university to its pre-war condition, but rebuilding it according to a new vision. The University of Khartoum, whose history dates back to 1902, had about 44,000 undergraduate and intermediate diploma students in 2025, as well as about 10,000 postgraduate students. It employed 5,501 staff, of whom academics accounted for 36% and non-academic employees 64%. The university includes 23 faculties, 12 research institutes, 10 research centres, four university hospitals, and five main campuses. Its housing facilities previously accommodated more than 20% of academic staff and senior employees, while it was linked to about 1,395 cooperating institutions through academic and research partnerships and agreements. items.title: Somalia president’s policies have failed the country, says academic
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – A prominent Somali professor has issued a sharp public rebuke of Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, warning that his administration’s policies have failed the country and accusing him of presiding over a political collapse that is pushing Somalis back toward tribal and regional allegiances. Afyare Elmi delivered the warning in an open […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – A prominent Somali professor has issued a sharp public rebuke of Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, warning that his administration’s policies have failed the country and accusing him of presiding over a political collapse that is pushing Somalis back toward tribal and regional allegiances. Afyare Elmi delivered the warning in an open letter posted to X on Monday, framing it as a direct appeal to the president to change course before, in his words, the country falls apart. “Almost a Full House” in 2022 Elmi opened his letter by recalling the breadth of political support present at Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s inauguration in the Halane area of Mogadishu. “On May 16, 2022, you assumed power with an almost full house. Only Somaliland, which has been seeking international recognition, and the extremist groups, which have been fighting the government, were not in the Halane tent. The rest were present at your inauguration,” Elmi wrote. That coalition, he said, has since collapsed. A Coalition in Retreat “Fast forward to today: the institutions are out of mandate, and you have lost many of the people and groups that were in the Halane tent in 2022,” Elmi wrote, adding that most of the politicians who backed the president’s 2022 victory — including figures from the national opposition, Puntland and Jubaland — are no longer part of the government. He pointed to specific flashpoints across the federal map: Southwest State is experiencing violent conflict, which Elmi attributed to “a poorly conceived and executed transition.” The principle of “do no harm,” which he described as foundational, has “been violated in a big way.” Galmudug and Hirshabelle are, in his words, “ticking time bombs that could explode in any direction.” “Mr. President, your policies have failed the country, and as a result, Somalis are now aligning with regional geopolitics along tribal and regional lines,” Elmi wrote. Elmi’s Prescription: Talks, Not Rhetoric Elmi argued that the way out of the crisis is for the president to recognize the danger the country faces and adopt what he called a pragmatic approach to resolving outstanding disputes “before it is too late.” He said the minimum the Somali public should expect is a credible and competitive political process open to all the actors who were present in 2022. “The time for empty rhetoric and gerrymandering or power-grabbing is over,” he wrote. “It is time to reach a political agreement with the opposition and reconcile with your opponents, both at the state and national levels. You must also return to the dispensation processes that Somalis have known and relied upon in the past.” He closed with a stark warning: “Otherwise, Somalia risks disintegration under your leadership, and such a legacy would be an unbearable burden to bear.” The letter lands as Somalia is contending in real time with escalating political disputes between the federal government in Mogadishu, several regional state administrations, and clan constituencies across the country.
