items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro departed Hargeisa on Thursday for a working visit to the United States, part of an effort to present the self-declared republic as an emerging power of geoeconomic and geosecurity value to Washington and other Western capitals, with particular emphasis on the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint. Officials said […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro departed Hargeisa on Thursday for a working visit to the United States, part of an effort to present the self-declared republic as an emerging power of geoeconomic and geosecurity value to Washington and other Western capitals, with particular emphasis on the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint. Officials said Irro will make a stopover in the United Arab Emirates en route to the US. The Somaliland leader is expected to pitch his territory’s importance to Washington on two fronts: its rare earth mineral deposits and its proximity to Yemen and the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint, a position officials believe could support a US military footing there and help counter threats from Houthi rebels. Somalia’s federal government has moved in parallel, dispatching a delegation led by Deputy Prime Minister Salah Jama on a counter-diplomacy push aimed at undercutting Irro’s Washington trip. The rival missions have drawn attention to the family ties binding the two camps. “For those who don’t know – Jama is actually from Somaliland and Irro’s kin,” said Rashid Abdi, a Horn of Africa analyst at Sahan Research. “Fascinating diplomacy,” Abdi added. Contact us: info@somaliguardian.com

items.body: Taemo Hadish is a farmer in Haweleti, in Raya Zebo, Tigray region. She says her cattle have become too weak to move because of a lack of fodder, while the farmland she relies on to feed her family have failed to grow. “We have not seen rain for the whole year,” she says. “Our animals are dying because there is nothing for them to eat.” The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has warned that parts of Ethiopia could experience below-average rainfall during the June–September rainy season as El Niño conditions develop. In northern Ethiopia, particularly Tigray, conflict-related disruptions to farming seasons have left 21 woredas at high risk of severe food insecurity, with 2.45 million people in need of emergency food assistance. Similar conditions are being reported in neighbouring Afar, where livestock are also dying as the drought worsens. According to a July FAO report, more than 18,000 livestock have died in Yaqer locality, Afar region, due to shortages of water and fodder. Farmers and woreda officials interviewed by the BBC say farmers in three woredas in Tigray region are struggling because of delayed rains linked to El Niño. The weather patterns have caused drought in the southern, south-eastern and central zones, while some woredas that received rainfall have experienced heavy hailstorms and flooding. In its May seasonal forecast, the Ethiopian Meteorology Institute warned that parts of southern and eastern Tigray, North and South Wollo, Afar and eastern Ethiopia were likely to receive below-average rainfall. It also forecast dry conditions in northern and eastern parts of the country in August. “We have never experienced a drought like this. There has not been enough rain, and we are going through a very difficult year,” says Alem Misgana, who lives in Alitena, in the Eastern Zone. Article in Amharic. items.title: Laftagaren forces attack Somali army positions in Baidoa again
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Heavy fighting erupted in Baidoa on Thursday after forces loyal to ousted Southwest State President Abdiasis Laftagaren attacked the city from multiple directions, seizing two federal army bases on its outskirts before entering the town and engaging government troops in fierce gun battles that lasted for hours. Laftagaren’s Darwish forces entered Baidoa […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Heavy fighting erupted in Baidoa on Thursday after forces loyal to ousted Southwest State President Abdiasis Laftagaren attacked the city from multiple directions, seizing two federal army bases on its outskirts before entering the town and engaging government troops in fierce gun battles that lasted for hours. Laftagaren’s Darwish forces entered Baidoa early in the morning, according to a spokesman for the forces, who said they would continue fighting until the last federal soldier leaves the region and control of the region is fully restored to its people. The forces later withdrew from the city, bringing the fighting to an end. Southwest State Information Minister Nur Sidow told reporters in Baidoa after the fighting that those who had attacked the city were Al-Shabaab , and said the assault had begun with suicide car bombs. The Somali federal government made a similar claim last month after Laftagaren’s forces launched another attack on Baidoa. Regional authorities and the federal government have yet to provide any tangible evidence for the assertion that the attackers were Al-Shabaab. The latest fighting left multiple people dead and caused other casualties, although there are no official figures. Among those killed was the commander of the personal guards of current Southwest leader Adan Madobe. Isaq Abdulle, commander of the Somali army’s 8th Brigade of the 60th Division, sustained serious injuries. Baidoa was once a relatively peaceful town under Laftagaren, but it has become a battleground since he was toppled. The repeated attacks by his forces have exposed the inability of the federal government and its Southwest allies to defend the city, even after thousands of troops were deployed there since March, analysts say. The latest assault highlights the continuing security crisis in Baidoa, where recurrent fighting has challenged the federal government’s control of the Southwest State capital. items.title: Sudan’s Sovereignty Council chief inspects army's readiness in Blue Nile State amid escalating clashes with RSF
items.summary: Abdel Fattah al-Burhan's visit comes amid escalating clashes between army, Raid Support Forces in Blue Nile State
items.body:
The chairman of Sudan’s Sovereign Council, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, inspected the readiness of the army on Wednesday in Blue Nile state in southeastern Sudan.

The visit comes amid escalating clashes in the state between the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N).

In a statement, the army’s 4th infantry division said that Burhan, who also commands the Sudanese army, visited the city of Damazin, the state capital and the headquarters of the division.

It added that Burhan inspected the division’s forces and assessed their combat readiness and preparedness to carry out their assigned missions.

He was also briefed on the security and operational situation in the region, according to the statement.

Burhan stressed “the need to raise levels of preparedness and vigilance and strengthen discipline and combat readiness," according to the statement.

He also called for “continuing to carry out missions in accordance with military plans and directives."

Burhan also inspected the military hospital in Damazin, where he was briefed on the conditions of wounded soldiers and patients, and the hospital’s operations.

He affirmed the army command’s commitment to its personnel and to providing them with the necessary care.

The statement quoted 4th Infantry Division Commander Maj. Gen. Ismail al-Tayeb, who said Burhan’s visit “enhanced their readiness to carry out their missions.”

“The division’s forces are fully prepared to perform their military duties, secure the region and protect civilians,” he said.

He added that the division was ready to “continue implementing the plans and directives issued by the command.”

Burhan’s visit comes amid rapidly developing military developments in Blue Nile state.

On Tuesday, the first contingent of joint forces from armed movements allied with the army arrived in Blue Nile state.

On Saturday, the army announced that it deployed an elite brigade affiliated with the General Intelligence Service to the battlefield in the Bakori axis in the state.

The RSF announced Friday that it seized the Bakori and Sarkam military bases southeast of Damazin.

The army also announced last Thursday that it had shot down a “hostile” drone in Blue Nile state after it crossed the border from Ethiopia.

It said it was the third drone it had announced shooting down within a week.

In addition to Blue Nile and the Darfur region in western Sudan, clashes have been ongoing in the three Kordofan states -- North, West and South Kordofan -- between the army and the RSF since Oct. 25.

Sudan has been witnessing a war between the army and the RSF since April 2023, which has killed tens of thousands and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Some of the militias, speaking to local media, said they oppose the elections b
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Armed militias seized centers designated for voter registration in Beledweyne on Tuesday, as Somalia’s electoral commission set September 30 for Hirshabelle municipal and parliamentary elections, intensifying opposition to the planned vote, Caasimada Online news website reported on Tuesday. Some of the militias, speaking to local media, said they oppose the elections being conducted by the government-appointed electoral commission. They said they would not accept a vote in which only one favored candidate is allowed to contest while all other candidates are banned, arguing that the process mirrors such an arrangement. The Somali federal government has not yet taken any action against the militias. The seizure comes as Hawadle clan politicians strongly oppose the planned Hirshabelle election, saying the process is not fair. They are also demanding their turn at the presidency of the Hirshabelle regional administration. The competing objections have placed the planned elections under heightened political tension in Beledweyne, where the seizure of the registration centers has directly disrupted locations designated for the electoral process. The militias’ opposition centers on what they describe as a process that favors one candidate while excluding others, while Hawadle politicians are challenging the fairness of the Hirshabelle election and pressing for their turn at the regional presidency. With the electoral commission having scheduled the Hirshabelle municipal and parliamentary elections for September 30, the dispute over the process remains unresolved, while the Somali federal government has yet to take action against the militias. items.title: Violent Clashes Stall School Reopenings in DRC
items.summary: Since at least 2025, hundreds of schoolchildren have been denied access to schools and educational facilities due to the violent clashes between the rebel groups and state forces. The resurgence of the Ebola virus has worsened the situation, as schools tried to reopen amid the disease outbreak. The post Violent Clashes Stall School Reopenings in DRC appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: Violent clashes between the Congolese armed forces and the M23 rebels have disrupted school reopenings in several localities in North Kivu in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). As the 2026-2027 academic year begins, schools have not yet reopened in several rural areas of the region, particularly in the Bankindi, Banamulema, and Balindu communities of the Kisimba tribal group. Just before the school year was set to begin, many families were forced to flee their homes to escape the intense fighting between the armed groups, particularly the Wazalendo militia, and the M23/AFC rebels in the region. Parents, students, and teachers have sought refuge to avoid the crossfire. Some families have taken shelter in the bushes, while others have relocated to towns like Pinga and Kalembe. The situation is severely compromising the normal reopening of school activities. For the displaced families, the immediate priority is survival, especially since they lack the means to pay school fees for their children. “We escaped with our children without carrying along our belongings. Today, we do not even know where we will sleep or what we will eat,” a parent taking refuge with his family in Pinga told HumAngle. “Under these conditions, it is difficult for us to think about school fees, uniforms or other school needs for our children. We very much wish for peace to return so that our children can return to school.” Some schools in Pinga have started admitting children of displaced families from zones affected by the fighting. A senior official from Kabeza Secondary School in Pinga, whose name is withheld for safety reasons, stated that the influx of students creates space issues, as the school must accommodate additional students from war-affected areas. “We are forced to welcome children from displaced families in order to enable them to continue their education. However, admitting them is not easy because some come without school requirements and their parents do not have the means to meet their needs. We demand assistance so that these children are not abandoned because of the war,” the official said. Faced with this situation, authorities in the education sector of the Walikale 3 sub-division are encouraging displaced parents to enrol their children in schools in their refuge zones, notably in Pinga and Kalembe, so they can continue schooling. Families hiding in bushes with their children, lacking access to schools, subsistence means, and essential services, are compromising their children’s educational futures. Since at least 2025, hundreds of schoolchildren have been denied access to schools and educational facilities due to the violent clashes between the rebel groups and state forces. The resurgence of the Ebola virus has worsened the situation, as schools tried to reopen amid the disease outbreak. The post Violent Clashes Stall School Reopenings in DRC appeared first on HumAngle .

items.title: Kidnapping on the Rise Near Cameroon’s Border with Nigeria
items.summary: The surge in kidnapping near Cameroon’s border with Nigeria coincides with several ongoing crises in the region. The post Kidnapping on the Rise Near Cameroon’s Border with Nigeria appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: A report from the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UNOCHA) has revealed that over 300 persons were kidnapped by terrorists in the Far North region of Cameroon during April, May, and June of 2026. In the same timeframe in 2025, 141 abductions were reported, which is a staggering 118 per cent increase in kidnappings. The recent report shows a serious decline in the region’s security landscape in the second quarter of 2026. During this period, 72 people were killed, and 48 were injured, which actually reflects a 6.5 per cent decrease in fatalities compared to the previous year, when 77 civilians lost their lives. The UNOCHA report stresses that understanding the worsening security situation in Far North Cameroon requires more than just looking at casualty numbers. Compared to the latter half of 2025, there were 167 more kidnappings, suggesting that abductions have become the major form of violence affecting communities near the Nigerian border. Beyond the loss of lives, terrorist operations in the region seem to have established a pervasive climate of fear, limiting movement and undermining the livelihood of local communities. The report states that such violence can lead to new displacements as people flee to areas deemed safer. For humanitarian organisations, the ongoing insecurity complicates efforts to deliver assistance to those in need. The report also noted a resurgence of improvised explosive devices (IEDs) in the Logone-et-Chari division, with two such incidents occurring between April and June this year. While the limited occurrences of IEDs do not definitively indicate a sustained reduction in violence, they add to the potential risks faced by residents and humanitarian workers, especially during periods of displacement in violence-affected areas. This surge in kidnappings coincides with several ongoing crises in the region. The UNOCHA report mentions new population displacements, a worsening measles outbreak, the emergence of cholera cases, and ongoing food insecurity. The post Kidnapping on the Rise Near Cameroon’s Border with Nigeria appeared first on HumAngle .

items.title: Somalia NSA confirms troops crossed into Ethiopia region
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia’s National Security Adviser, Aways Haji Yusuf, on Tuesday confirmed for the first time that an undisclosed number of Somali National Army (SNA) troops who recently completed a Saudi Arabia-funded training program in Hanaanbure, Galmudug, have crossed into Ethiopia’s Somali region. Yusuf said the soldiers, who had undergone more than a year […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia’s National Security Adviser, Aways Haji Yusuf, on Tuesday confirmed for the first time that an undisclosed number of Somali National Army (SNA) troops who recently completed a Saudi Arabia-funded training program in Hanaanbure, Galmudug, have crossed into Ethiopia’s Somali region. Yusuf said the soldiers, who had undergone more than a year of training, were granted leave to visit their families and that the federal government is aware of their presence in the region for that purpose. “If there are other issues, we will let you (media) know,” Yusuf told reporters. Defection Reports Preceded the Admission The confirmation comes days after multiple Somali media outlets, including outlets based in Ethiopia’s Somali region, reported that dozens of soldiers – part of a cohort of 3,000 trained at Hananbure – had defected and were subsequently captured by regional forces before being taken to Jigjiga. Reported figures for the number involved have varied widely across outlets, with some citing 300, others 180, and others as high as 900. None of these figures has been independently confirmed, and it remains unclear whether the soldiers defected or were simply on approved leave to visit their families, as the government maintains. Analyst: Admission “Likely to Generate More Questions” A Nairobi-based Horn of Africa analyst with Sahan Research described the National Security Adviser’s admission as “refreshing and commendable, but likely to generate more questions.” “Did Somalia recruit forces from the Somali Regional State of Ethiopia with permission from regional and federal authorities? If not, how will Addis Ababa respond?” the analyst asked. A Backdrop of Strained Ties The episode unfolds against a backdrop of strained relations between Mogadishu and Addis Ababa in recent years, with the two governments aligned to separate geopolitical camps. Ethiopia has increasingly sided with the United Arab Emirates, including in its support for the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan, while Somalia has increasingly aligned itself with Saudi Arabia and Turkey. items.title: 22,000 displaced by fighting in Sudan’s Blue Nile state in last week: UN
items.summary: Agency says civilians fleeing violence in Geissan district have sought safety in several areas, including state capital Ed Damazine
items.body:
About 22,000 people have been displaced from Sudan’s Blue Nile state in the last week as fighting intensified in the Geissan district, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said Tuesday.

OCHA said in a statement that continued violence is putting civilians at risk and forcing thousands to flee their homes.

“In Blue Nile State, local authorities report that nearly 22,000 people may have been displaced in the past seven days due to escalating fighting in the locality of Geissan,” it said.

The statement said that “many are sheltering in schools or have fled to other areas, including towards the state capital, Ed Damazine.”

The Geissan Emergency Room, a local aid body, said Sunday that nearly 20,000 people had fled the area of Medina 12 in the Geissan district because of the fighting and worsening security conditions.

Blue Nile has seen a new escalation in the last two days after the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North launched attacks in several areas of the state.

OCHA also said attacks on Saturday on villages north and northwest of El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, caused casualties and displaced civilians, amid reports that civilian property and livestock were looted.

“In West Darfur State, civilians were reportedly killed and injured when a drone strike hit a fuel market in Adekong, near the border with Chad, last Thursday. The attack also damaged civilian property,” it said.

OCHA renewed its demand for all parties to the conflict “to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, respect international humanitarian law, and allow humanitarian organizations to operate safely and independently.”

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Monday that 450 people were displaced from the village of al-Qardud Abu Zeid in the al-Rahad district of North Kordofan because of deteriorating security in a single day.

Alongside Blue Nile and Darfur, fighting has continued since Oct. 25 in Sudan’s three Kordofan states -- North Kordofan, West Kordofan and South Kordofan -- between the army and the RSF.

Sudan has been at war between the army and the RSF since April 2023. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced about 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

items.title: Terrorism forces 57 primary schools to shut in Nigeria’s Borno, 80 students remain captive: Official
items.summary: Soldiers have been deployed in Mussa and Lassa alongside local vigilantes.
items.body:
At least 57 primary schools are currently not functioning in Nigeria’s northeastern Borno State due to insecurity, while about 80 students abducted during attacks on schools remain in captivity, according to local education authorities.

The situation was disclosed by Fasuma Askira, education secretary of Askira-Uba Local Government Area, where only 56 of the 113 primary schools are currently operating.

On May 15, terrorists attacked Mussa Central Primary School and abducted dozens of children. Although the exact number remains disputed, the Borno State Government has more recently put the number of missing pupils at about 44.

On June 29, insurgents attacked Government Day Secondary School in Lassa while students were sitting for a National Examinations Council examination. Some students were subsequently rescued, but 36 students and a teacher remained in captivity.

Combining the latest government estimate from Mussa with the verified Lassa figure puts the number of students still in captivity at about 80.

As of Aug. 31, the children abducted from Mussa had spent 108 days in captivity, while the Lassa students had been held for 63 days.

Simon Waindu, whose daughter is among the Lassa students, said none of the children had returned and that families had received no information about their rescue.

Meanwhile, authorities have closed schools in communities affected by insecurity. Authorities have also proposed the deployment of community vigilantes around schools when classes resume, while soldiers have been deployed in Mussa and Lassa alongside local vigilantes.

The latest developments come after Anadolu reported in June that terrorists abducted six women and two babies near the scene of a school attack in Borno state.

The incident occurred shortly after suspected insurgents attacked Government Day Secondary School in Lassa while students were taking examinations, further highlighting the vulnerability of civilians around schools in the conflict-affected region.

Nigeria's northeastern states have faced more than a decade of insurgency, with Boko Haram and ISWAP among the armed groups responsible for attacks, abductions and displacement.

The continued captivity of students and closure of schools raise concerns over the long-term educational consequences of the conflict, particularly for children in communities already affected by displacement and poverty.

items.title: Displacement and the Right to Vote: Addressing the Exclusion of Nigeria’s IDPs in the 2027 GeneralElections
items.summary: Introduction Between April 2025 and June 2026, over 2.3 million internally displaced people (IDPs) were identified by the International Organisation for Migration’s 51st DTM Site Assessment. The data highlights a 2% increase from Round 50 of the assessment. The number represents a population of Nigerians covered by the constitution and, specifically, the National Policy on […] The post Displacemen
items.body: Introduction Between April 2025 and June 2026, over 2.3 million internally displaced people (IDPs) were identified by the International Organisation for Migration’s 51st DTM Site Assessment. The data highlights a 2% increase from Round 50 of the assessment. The number represents a population of Nigerians covered by the constitution and, specifically, the National Policy on IDPs to restore their rights, agency and dignity. Mostly uprooted by long-running conflicts, HumAngle found that IDPs across various communities are being pushed outside the map of the 2027 electoral processes, denying them the opportunity to exercise their rights and exposing systemic failure and neglect. What’s New? HumAngle travelled to rural communities and town centres where IDPs are hosted. Across communities in Adamawa, Borno and Katsina states, there is a pattern of recurring barriers to IDPs’ electoral participation . These include incomplete voter registration exercises, difficulty replacing or transferring Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs), limited voter education, lack of information about registration procedures, the cost and insecurity associated with travelling to original polling units, and declining confidence in the electoral process. Key findings HumAngle identifies a policy gap in the management of IDP challenges. The National Policy on IDPs says all rights contained in the Nigerian constitution and humanitarian instruments are to be enjoyed by IDPs. Yet, this has not been the case across many IDP camps. There are practical barriers to voter registration. Often, due to logistical failure to reach IDP camps and the poor implementation of the Independent National Electoral Commission’s IDPs Voting Regulations . IDPs have demonstrated their desire for inclusion and participation in electoral processes, with many first-time voters hoping to be enrolled in the voter register. Voter education and information gaps in IDP communities persist. IDPs with lost or damaged voter cards do not know how to get a replacement, while INEC’s online self-service option is ineffective due to the digital gaps in IDP and conflict-affected communities. No polling infrastructure within IDP camps. Where field visits were conducted, IDPs who have their voter cards have to go back to communities they fled to vote, further exposing them to the risks of harm. Why does it matter? Inclusion is crucial for a constitutional democracy and a nation attempting to heal from radicalisation. In this context, it restores confidence in the state and gives agency to citizens who are in their most vulnerable state. Invariably, this enhances recovery, and restores a sense of belonging for a population that seems to exist in limbo. Social recovery does not work in isolation. It has to be a whole approach, and INEC’s voter registration and participation in elections by IDPs is part of this larger process of recovery and agency-giving for IDPs. The integrity of electoral processes is only intact when no one feels excluded. What can be done INEC should create a special window urgently to regularise IDPs, register those of voting age with a special target to first-time voters across identified communities. This will enable the completion of registration, enrolment of new voters, and replacement of lost or damaged cards ahead of the 2027 elections. INEC should revamp its voter education campaign through collaboration with the National Orientation Agency and Local Government Community Development Departments to reach IDPs with clear and needed voter education and information. Civil society and the media should continue independent monitoring and reporting on voter registration and election-related exercises to keep issues visible to policymakers and the public. Humanitarian and camp management actors should integrate voter education activities within camp programmes to bridge awareness gaps. They should also leverage existing camp leadership structures to coordinate with INEC, schedule visits and follow up. The National Commission for Refugees, Migrants and Internally Displaced Persons (NCFRMI) should review the National IDP Policy and develop a complementary national framework that elaborately operationalises how the participation of IDPs in elections should henceforth be governed. Conclusion The 2027 general election is near, and IDPs, especially first-time voters, are enthusiastic and hopeful to participate in a civic exercise. The constitution granted them the right; the laws and policies empower them with the opportunity, but the system is locking them out. This clash between policy and practice has consequences. It disenfranchises and breeds national grievances where healing, recovery and agency should take centre. INEC and all relevant stakeholders have a role to reverse the dying hope for inclusion, stronger democracy and electoral integrity. Further reading Nigeria’s Displaced Communities Risk Being Shut Out of Elections, https://www.humanglemedia.com/nigerias-displaced-communities-risk-being-shut-out-of-elections Regulations for Voting by Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs), https://www.inecnigeria.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/REGULATIONS.pdf Acknowledgment This policy brief was made possible through the dedication of a talented team of professionals, led by Abdussamad Ahmad Yusuf, for the research, analysis, and drafting of this document. The post Displacement and the Right to Vote: Addressing the Exclusion of Nigeria’s IDPs in the 2027 GeneralElections appeared first on HumAngle .

items.title: Italy Expands Police Training Support for Somalia
items.summary: Talyaaniga ayaa Muqdisho ku shaaciyay qorshe lagu xoojinayo iskaashiga amni ee Soomaaliya, iyadoo diiradda la saarayo tababarka booliiska, dhismaha hay’adaha amniga iyo ka hortagga xagjirnimada. The post Italy Expands Police Training Support for Somalia first appeared on Radio Dalsan .
items.body: Italy expands police training and security support for Somalia Italian Ambassador Pier Mario Daccò Coppi says Rome will deepen its cooperation with Somalia on police training, institutional development and efforts to prevent violent extremism. MOGADISHU, September 1, 2026 — Italy has pledged to strengthen its support for Somalia’s security institutions, with an emphasis on police training, stabilisation and government-led projects in communities affected by conflict.Speaking at Somalia’s National Internal Security Conference in Mogadishu, Italian Ambassador Pier Mario Daccò Coppi described the gathering as an important opportunity to bring together the political and institutional leadership of the internal security sector The two-day conference brings together representatives of the federal government and federal member states to discuss security governance, institutional coordination and the supervisory role of the Ministry of Internal Security.Daccò Coppi said Somalia was making important progress in institution-building and stabilisation, although the process remained gradual. Longstanding police and security cooperation The ambassador described relations between Italy and Somalia as a historic partnership that had endured the instability and conflict of Somalia’s recent past. He said Italy’s policy was guided by support for Somalia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, security and stabilisation. The two countries have maintained a defence cooperation framework since 2013. The Italian Carabinieri began training members of the Somali Police Force’s Darwish units in Djibouti in 2014. According to the Italian Ministry of Defence, the MIADIT programme trained 3,100 Somali police personnel over its first 10 years. The courses cover law enforcement, stability policing and responses to high-risk security incidents. Italian Ministry of Defence Italy also participates in three European Union operations linked to Somalia: EUTM Somalia, EUCAP Somalia and Operation Atalanta.EUTM supports military training, EUCAP helps strengthen civilian law-enforcement capacity, and Atalanta focuses on maritime security and counter-piracy operations. Five-year police training framework Daccò Coppi highlighted a memorandum signed in Mogadishu on July 3, 2026, by Somali Internal Security Minister Abdullahi Sheikh Ismail Fartag and Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi.The memorandum creates a government-to-government framework for vocational and academic police training, train-the-trainer programmes, study visits, exchanges and the sharing of professional expertise.It also establishes a joint working group responsible for coordinating implementation, reviewing progress and planning future activities.The framework will remain in force for an initial five years and may be renewed through the written consent of both governments. Somalia’s Ministry of Internal Security The ambassador said a further agreement on police training was expected to follow. He added that broader cooperation between the two countries’ police institutions would support efforts against transnational organised crime, irregular migration and terrorism. No date or detailed terms for the expected follow-up agreement were announced. Preventing violent extremism Daccò Coppi argued that force and legislation alone were not sufficient to counter violent extremism.He said security measures should be accompanied by efforts to address social and economic conditions that can contribute to radicalisation.The ambassador connected this approach to the Towards Peace and Stability in Somalia , or TPSS, programme launched by Italy and the Federal Government of Somalia.Under the initiative, Somali authorities identify priority interventions, while Italy provides funding for projects intended to strengthen services and stability in vulnerable areas. Health projects in three districts Somalia’s Office of the Prime Minister selected health projects in three districts: Afmadow in Jubaland Harardhere in Galmudug Adale in Hirshabeelle In Adale, the programme will rehabilitate and bring Sheikh Ahmed Gabyow Hospital into operation. The district has a population of approximately 100,000 people, including internally displaced communities.The TPSS programme has an initial budget of €3.82 million. It is financed by Italy and implemented by the Somali Prime Minister’s Office. Italian Agency for Development Cooperation Daccò Coppi said he hoped the conference would strengthen institutional coordination and improve the capabilities of Somalia’s security forces.He said the long-term objective was for Somali institutions to assume full responsibility for national security through the lawful, legitimate and accountable use of force. The post Italy Expands Police Training Support for Somalia first appeared on Radio Dalsan .

items.title: Türkiye pledges continued security and economic support for Somalia
items.summary: Danjiraha Turkiga Alper Aktaş oo ka hadlaya Shirweynaha Qaran ee Amniga Gudaha ee Muqdisho The post Türkiye pledges continued security and economic support for Somalia first appeared on Radio Dalsan .
items.body: Turkish Ambassador Alper Aktaş says Ankara will maintain its support for Somali security forces while expanding cooperation in energy, fisheries and other strategic sectors. MOGADISHU, September 1, 2026 — Türkiye has pledged to continue supporting Somalia’s security institutions, counterterrorism operations and long-term economic development as the country works towards greater self-sufficiency.Addressing Somalia’s National Internal Security Conference in Mogadishu, Turkish Ambassador Alper Aktaş said the country had made visible security progress, although significant challenges and uncertainties remained.Aktaş said his more than two and a half years in Somalia had allowed him to witness changes in Mogadishu firsthand. “Just a few years ago, Mogadishu was associated with major explosions, instability and persistent conflict,” he said. “Today, we speak of rising skyscrapers, ambitious development projects and genuine hope.” Training for Gorgor and Haramcad units The ambassador said Türkiye-trained Gorgor special forces continued to take part in operations against terrorist groups.He added that Türkiye was also training specialised Haramcad units within the Somali Police Force.According to Aktaş, more than 1,000 personnel have been trained and are helping respond to security threats in Somali cities. He did not provide a breakdown of the personnel, the period covered by the figure or their current deployments.Türkiye opened its largest overseas military base in Mogadishu in 2017 and provides training to both the Somali military and police. Air support for security operations Aktaş said Türkiye had increased its air assets in Somalia at the request of Somali authorities to support operations on the ground.He said the additional support was already contributing to counterterrorism efforts. However, he did not identify the aircraft involved, disclose their number or provide independently verifiable information about their operational impact.Further information from the Somali and Turkish authorities would therefore be needed to establish the scope and results of the deployment. Connecting security with economic development The ambassador argued that security gains would not be sustainable without economic progress. He linked Türkiye’s security engagement to its growing involvement in Somalia’s energy, fisheries and infrastructure sectors.Aktaş referred to the continuing work of the Çağrı Bey deep-sea drilling vessel, planned fisheries initiatives and a proposed spaceport project.The Çağrı Bey arrived off Mogadishu in April 2026 to begin Türkiye’s first overseas deep-sea oil exploration project. The planned well is expected to reach a depth of 7,500 metres, while the drilling operation was projected to last about 10 months.The operation follows an intergovernmental energy agreement signed in March 2024 covering the exploration, evaluation, development and production of oil and gas in Somalia’s offshore and onshore areas. Exploratory drilling does not, however, guarantee the discovery of commercially recoverable oil. The results of the well, the possible size of any reserves and the eventual financial benefits for Somalia have not yet been announced. Commitment to continued partnership Aktaş said international partners should maintain their assistance as Somalia moves towards greater self-reliance. “Türkiye remains fully committed to doing its part,” he said. He concluded by thanking Somalia’s security institutions and described the country as a second home for himself and his family.His remarks presented Türkiye’s engagement as a broad partnership spanning security, defence, energy and economic development. Some proposed initiatives, particularly the spaceport, still require further official details concerning financing, implementation agreements and timelines. The post Türkiye pledges continued security and economic support for Somalia first appeared on Radio Dalsan .

items.title: Somalia Sets September 30 for Galmudug, Hirshabelle Elections
items.summary: The elections hold broader significance for Somalia's political stability. Federal member state elections are crucial for establishing legitimate regional administrations that can partner with the federal government on security, development, and constitutional reform. Any delays or disputes could undermine progress toward the national elections scheduled for 2027. Both elections will proceed simul
items.body: Electoral commission announces fresh polls for two federal member states following court ruling that annulled Galmudug’s previous results. Mogadishu – Somalia’s Independent National Electoral and Boundaries Commission has scheduled September 30, 2026, as polling day for local council and parliamentary elections in Galmudug and Hirshabelle. The commission released separate electoral timelines for both federal member states on Tuesday, marking a significant step toward completing the country’s ongoing regional election process. The decision comes after Somalia’s Supreme Court annulled Galmudug’s previous election results on August 23, citing irregularities in the electoral process. This ruling forced the federal member state to conduct fresh polls, adding pressure on the electoral commission to deliver credible and transparent elections within a compressed timeframe. Hirshabelle, meanwhile, will proceed with its scheduled elections as originally planned. Galmudug’s electoral calendar begins on September 10, when the commission will designate polling centers and voting stations. Political associations must submit their candidate lists by September 20, followed by the accreditation of party agents and observers on September 26. The shortened timeline reflects the urgency of completing the process after the court’s intervention. Campaign activities will conclude on September 28, two days before polling day. Hirshabelle’s electoral process started earlier, with the publication of a preliminary voter register on September 2. The commission will subsequently establish polling stations, register voters, distribute voter cards, and verify candidate lists. Political associations will announce their candidates on September 22, followed by the accreditation of party agents and observers. Campaigning will end on September 28. “These elections represent an important opportunity for citizens in Galmudug and Hirshabelle to exercise their democratic rights,” a senior electoral official told this reporter on condition of anonymity. The official emphasized the commission’s commitment to transparency and fairness. The elections hold broader significance for Somalia’s political stability. Federal member state elections are crucial for establishing legitimate regional administrations that can partner with the federal government on security, development, and constitutional reform. Any delays or disputes could undermine progress toward the national elections scheduled for 2027. Both elections will proceed simultaneously on September 30, with results expected shortly thereafter. The post Somalia Sets September 30 for Galmudug, Hirshabelle Elections first appeared on Radio Dalsan .

[…] The post SNA brobes video of soldiers suffocating
items.body: Somalia’s military opened a preliminary investigation on Tuesday after a video circulated online appeared to show members of the Somali National Army (SNA) abusing a man in custody during an operation against Al-Shabaab, the SNAF Command said in a statement, adding that the footage contravenes its Code of Conduct and the laws of armed conflict. The probe lands at a sensitive moment for Somalia’s armed forces, which are locked in an intensifying offensive against Al-Shabaab across multiple regions. Any confirmed breach of prisoner-of-war protections could complicate ties with international partners who fund and train SNAF units, and would test the military’s willingness to discipline its own ranks publicly. The footage, widely shared on social media, shows uniformed men believed to be Somali soldiers surrounding a young man who appears to be in custody. The men are seen placing a plastic bag over the prisoner’s head, apparently suffocating him, triggering widespread condemnation online. The SNAF Command said the investigation would determine the circumstances of the incident and identify those responsible. “The SNAF Command strongly warns all personnel against engaging in such conduct,” the military said in its statement. The statement did not name any soldiers shown in the video, nor did it disclose where or when the incident occurred. It also did not clarify the identity or current condition of the man seen being held. Officials said personnel found to have violated prisoner-of-war protections or broader human rights standards would face both legal and military disciplinary action. “Firm legal and military disciplinary action will be taken against anyone found to have violated the laws of armed conflict, the rights of prisoners of war or human rights,” the statement said. Rights monitors and international law experts have indirectly noted that mistreatment of detainees during counter-insurgency operations can undermine both battlefield legitimacy and cooperation with foreign backers, according to [source/report, if available]. The SNAF has not said whether any soldiers have been arrested or suspended pending the outcome of the investigation. The case comes as Somali government troops and allied fighters continue offensives against Al-Shabaab in multiple regions, part of a broader campaign to reclaim territory from the militant group. The post SNA brobes video of soldiers suffocating bound Al-Shabaab suspect first appeared on Radio Dalsan .

items.title: DR Congo Ebola cases jump above 6,000
items.summary: Since outbreak declaration in May, virus has killed more than 2,900 people in Congo, according to health authorities
items.body:
Confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo surpassed 6,000 on Monday as authorities intensified efforts to contain the outbreak, official data showed.

Congo has reported 6,041 cases, including 2,911 deaths, since the outbreak was declared in mid-May, according to the Health Ministry’s latest situation update.

At least 1,366 people have recovered, while 619 patients remain in isolation or hospital.

The latest Ebola outbreak in Congo is the world’s second-largest by recorded infections, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, has affected 60 health zones across six provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele and Tshopo.

The ministry said response efforts remain concentrated in areas with active transmission, with particular attention to Ituri, which accounts for the majority of cases and affected health zones.

The rise in cases and wider geographic spread over the past three months represent a “substantial increase” in the scale of the outbreak, according to the WHO.

The government has rolled out an Ebola vaccination campaign targeting health and frontline workers.

The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) announced last week a new $16.5 million partnership with African biopharmaceutical company Minapharm Group to develop its Bundibugyo vaccine candidate.

items.title: 200 fighters defect from Sudan's paramilitary RSF, join army: State media
items.summary: Latest defection follows departure of hundreds of fighters, several commanders from paramilitary group in recent weeks
items.body:
A force of 200 fighters has defected from Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and joined the Sudanese army, state media reported Sunday.

The group, which included prominent field commanders, arrived in Omdurman, west of the capital Khartoum, according to the state-run Sudan News Agency.

The force was led by Abu Bakr Hamouda Dahloop, commander of the special missions intelligence division in North Kordofan state, the agency said.

The group announced that it was joining the Sudanese army with all its equipment and was ready to take part in combat operations alongside the military and allied forces.

Dahloop said the fighters had realized "their mistake in following the project being implemented by the RSF militia."

He said they had joined the "national camp" and would fight "for the demands of the Sudanese people to eliminate the rebel RSF militia."

The latest move follows several other reported defections from the RSF in recent weeks.

On Aug. 19, Sudanese authorities announced that four military commanders, 318 fighters and 50 combat vehicles had defected from the RSF.

That group, led by Lt. Col. Musa Ali Ahmed, known as "Khamsin," joined the army, according to authorities.

On Aug. 13, authorities said another RSF force comprising 21 commanders and 270 fighters had defected and joined the army.

The RSF has also seen defections among senior field and political figures, including Fares Al-Nour, political adviser to the RSF commander; Maj. Gen. Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, known as "Al-Nour Al-Qubba"; and field commander Ali Rizqallah, known as "Savanna."

The three Kordofan states -- North, West and South -- have witnessed clashes between the army and the RSF since October 2025.

Sudan has been embroiled in war between the army and the RSF since April 2023. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

items.title: Imported From Egypt: The Extremist Ideology That Inspired Boko Haram
items.summary: This is the story of how modern Islamist extremism emerged from the edge of an African prison and moved into Nigeria, escalating into an unending fire of insurgency. The post Imported From Egypt: The Extremist Ideology That Inspired Boko Haram appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: In August 2016, Mamman Nur, one of Boko Haram’s foremost commanders , dramatically sat before a camera on the shore of the Sambisa Forest, a vast terrorist hideout in North East Nigeria. He publicly accused the group’s supreme leader, Abubakar Shekau, of doctrinal deviance and transgressions. He said Abubakar had become power-drunk, killing his own commanders over minor disagreements and spilling the blood of fellow Muslims. He named several terrorist figures Shekau had killed, including Mustapha Chad, Abu Amr Falluja, Kaka Allai and Mallam Ba’ana Banki. He titled the recording Exposé , deliberately weaponising the same word Shekau had used to attack his critics. He also invoked the words of the former Islamic State spokesman Abu Muhammad al-Adnani , saying: “Whoever changes, we will also change him.” His message was not only a threat; it was also a campaign to depose Shekau as the leader of the terror group. Within months, Mamman’s faction formally broke away to become the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), as Shekau led the Jama’atu Ahlussunnah Lidda’awati wal Jihad (JAS). This movement had existed before Boko Haram pledged allegiance to the Islamic State. Behind the sudden division lay an unfolding theological debate within the global Salafi-jihadi movements for decades. It revolved around one question that has repeatedly divided jihadist organisations from the Middle East to the Lake Chad Basin: How far can the practice of takfir – declaring other Muslims as non-believers – go before this doctrine, which is meant to validate jihad, starts to undermine the very concept of jihad itself? Drawing on Boko Haram’s internal correspondence, Arabic treatises, multimedia recordings, and local sermons, HumAngle traces how an ideology born in Egypt travelled through Jordan, Iraq, and Syria before taking root in northeastern Nigeria. What later appeared as a personal power struggle between Shekau and Mamman Nur was, in reality, the culmination of a decades-long ideological dispute over faith, authority, governance, and the limits of violence. The journey that turned the former terrorist allies into bitter enemies began several decades back, in an Egyptian prison cell. Sayyid Qutb: Reinventing the concept of jahiliyya A popular photo of Sayyid Qutb while in detention in Egypt. Source: ABC News The story begins with Sayyid Qutb, an Egyptian author and one of the foremost figures in modern Sunni Islamic revivalism. He’s the author of a popular Islamist book, Ma’alim fi al-Tariq, mostly known as Milestones , which he wrote while in prison under the Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser, and published shortly before his execution in 1966. The book was said to have transformed a classical Islamic concept into a revolutionary political doctrine. The term “jahiliyya” literally referred to the pre-Islamic Arabian era before the Prophet Muhammad’s message, but Sayyid gave it a radically different meaning in his book. He argued that contemporary Muslim societies had fallen back into a new jahiliyya because they accepted political systems that placed human authority above divine law. Sayyid firmly believes that sovereignty is solely God’s domain. He argues that any government that creates laws outside of Sharia, even if its leaders identify as Muslims, is essentially practising a modern form of paganism. The solution, he claimed, was the emergence of a committed Islamic leadership capable of separating itself from corrupt society before working to transform it. That radical framework would become one of the most influential ideas in contemporary jihadist literature. Variations of it would later appear in the writings and speeches of militant organisations from Egypt and Jordan to Iraq, Syria, and Nigeria. The book’s influence on Boko Haram was neither indirect nor accidental. Mohammed Yusuf, Boko Haram’s founder, openly defended Sayyid against critics within Nigeria’s Salafi movement. In one of the sermons reproduced in The Boko Haram Reader, a book edited by Abdulbasit Kassim and Michael Nwankpa, Yusuf warned his followers against reading books that dismissed Sayyid and Hasan al-Banna , the founder of the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational Sunni Islamist organisation founded in Egypt in 1928. He praised Sayyid as a scholar whom Allah had granted a unique understanding of communism and what he described as polytheistic political systems. Citing the Albanian-born Syrian Hadith scholar Muhammad Nasir al-Din al-Albani , he argued that no contemporary scholar had explained the meaning of la ilaha illa Allah (there is no god but Allah) as comprehensively as Sayyid had in his book, Milestones. He also claimed that Sayyid’s writings played a role in inspiring Osama bin Laden. Throughout much of his public preaching, the Boko Haram founder portrayed himself as someone restoring the original teachings of Islam rather than introducing new doctrines. However, his sermons revealed that one of the intellectual foundations of his terrorist organisation had been laid decades earlier by an Egyptian author, who had written from prison. Although Sayyid didn’t create Boko Haram, he introduced the conceptual language that jihadist ideologues expanded, refined, and eventually transported into northeastern Nigeria. From diagnosis to doctrine Abu Muhammad Al-Maqdisi, a Salafi-Jihadi ideologue who is the key intellectual of modern jihadism. Source: Wikipedia While Sayyid seemed to have established the groundwork for radical jihadist ideologies, Abu Muhammad al-Maqdisi, a Palestinian writer and Salafi Islamist , developed the legal framework. Born in 1959, the Jordanian ideologue emerged during the 1980s as one of the most influential theorists of modern Salafi-jihadism. His book Millat Ibrahim (The Religion of Abraham), completed in 1984, built on Sayyid’s concepts of sovereignty, transforming them into a practical doctrine. Abu Muhammad argued that leaders who chose to govern by conventional, secular laws, instead of divine revelation, have deviated from the teachings of Islam, and therefore have abandoned the religion. From this, he developed the concept of takfir al-hukkam (declaring such rulers as apostates) and the doctrine of al-wala’ wal-bara’ (complete loyalty to believers and total disavowal of unbelievers, their institutions, and political systems). In his publication with the Combating Terrorism Centre , Joas Wagemakers, an associate professor of Islamic and Arabic Studies at Utrecht University, stated that Abu Muhammad was the first prominent Islamist to publicly declare the Saudi ruling family apostate for embracing the idea of democracy. His influence spread far beyond his own extremist writings. In the mid-1990s, he met a young Jordanian militant named Ahmad Fadil al-Khalayleh, better known as Abu Mus’ab al-Zarqawi , in prison. The two spent years together in detention, with Abu Muhammad serving as Abu Musab’s principal ideological mentor. When Abu Musab later established al-Qaeda in Iraq after the U.S. invasion of 2003, he carried much of that intellectual framework with him. The relationship eventually became the first major case study of a pattern that would later recur within Boko Haram. Abu Mus’ab Al-Zarqawi. Source: The Guardian By 2004, Abu Mus’ab had taken the excommunication doctrine far beyond what his teacher considered acceptable. His campaign against Iraqi Shiites relied on mass excommunication and indiscriminate violence, treating entire communities as legitimate military targets. Abu Muhammad publicly objected to his approach. After his release from prison in July 2005, he told Al Jazeera that it was “forbidden to equate the ordinary Shiite with the Americans in warfare”. His objection was not over the legitimacy of jihad itself but over the widening circle of Muslims being declared unbelievers. Abu Mus’ab rejected the criticism, claiming his mentor’s intervention harmed the jihad in Iraq instead of resolving it. The dispute would soon draw the attention of al-Qaeda’s top leaders. In July 2005, Ayman al-Zawahiri, then Osama bin Laden’s deputy, sent Abu Mus’ab a letter that has since become one of the movement’s most important internal documents. Ayman warned that the indiscriminate killing of Shiite civilians was alienating ordinary Muslims and undermining al-Qaeda’s broader objectives. He questioned why Iraqi Shiites should be targeted wholesale when many could be excused because of ignorance. This theological qualification would later reappear almost verbatim in Boko Haram’s own internal correspondence. The disagreement established a pattern that resurfaced repeatedly over the next decades. First, an ideologue developed the doctrine. Then a militant commander applied the doctrine more aggressively than its authors. Finally, an internal rebellion argued that the doctrine itself had been pushed beyond its limits. Years later, Boko Haram replayed almost the same sequence. How the ideology moved to Maiduguri Muhammad Yusuf during a pre

items.title: Algeria sends 4 fighter jets to Niger after unrest in Niamey
items.summary: 2 patrols comprising 4 Sukhoi Su-30 aircraft land at Niamey airport, accompanied by aerial refueling plane, says Defense Ministry
items.body:
Algeria sent four fighter jets to Niger on Sunday following recent unrest in the capital Niamey, the Defense Ministry said.

The ministry said two patrols comprising four Sukhoi Su-30 aircraft landed at Niamey airport, accompanied by an aerial refueling plane.

The aircraft were deployed at the request of Nigerien authorities on “a mission to support the Nigerien army in confronting an attempt to destabilize the brotherly state of Niger,” it added.

The deployment was ordered by Algerian Army Chief of Staff Said Chengriha under instructions from President Abdelmadjid Tebboune to strengthen strategic cooperation between Algeria and Niger, “particularly in the military field.”

The ministry said the operation “reaffirms Algeria’s firm commitment and determination to continue its efforts to strengthen security and stability in the region.”

It also renewed Algeria’s “constant support for the government and people of Niger in overcoming this sensitive period.”

Nigerien Prime Minister Ali Mahamane Lamine Zeine received the Algerian mission and expressed “his thanks and gratitude” to Tebboune and the Algerian people for the support, according to the statement.

The recent unrest included attacks around Diori Hamani International Airport and Air Base 101, a strategic military facility in Niamey, as well as other sites in the capital.

Niger's defense minister said military activity in the capital Niamey had been brought under control and security forces had regained control of critical sites that were targeted.

items.title: US welcomes Obasanjo’s Tigray visit as fears of renewed conflict grow
items.summary: The US embassy in Ethiopia says it has been encouraged by former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo’s visit to Mekelle yesterday. Tensions between the Tigrayan authorities and Ethiopia’s federal government have remained high for mo
items.body: The US embassy in Ethiopia says it has been encouraged by former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo’s visit to Mekelle yesterday. In a statement, US Ambassador Ervin Massinga said Mr Obasanjo’s work under his African Union mandate was critical at a time of mounting concern over renewed fighting. Tensions between the Tigrayan authorities and Ethiopia’s federal government have remained high for months, fuelling fears that the conflict could once again erupt into war. Mr Massinga said all sides should instead focus on addressing the drought conditions affecting communities across the country, as millions of people across the region face acute hunger. The Greater Horn of Africa is enduring one of its worst droughts in decades, compounded by years of conflict and instability and the effects of a strengthening El Niño event. “Getting people home and back to their productive lives, safely and with dignity, should be the objective of all leaders, and that will take compromise,” he said. “We look forward to engaging former President Obasanjo on this matter of critical importance to the future of the people of Ethiopia,” Mr Massing added. However, TPLF leaders say Mr Obasanjo’s visit to Mekelle “produced no new proposals or tangible progress towards dialogue with the Ethiopian federal government.” In a statement issued today, the TPLF said Mr Obasanjo’s visit was made without a prior appointment, but that Tigray’s president rearranged his schedule to meet him. During the meeting, the TPLF “expressed disappointment over what it described as a lack of meaningful follow-up to discussions held in June, when several issues were identified as potential entry points for dialogue” with the federal government. items.title: At least Six Dead in Addis Traffic Accident
items.summary: ADDIS ABABA – A traffic accident involving a minbus and an excavator claimed the lives of at least six people in Addis Ababa on Monday, according to a
items.body: ADDIS ABABA – A traffic accident involving a minbus and an excavator claimed the lives of at least six people in Addis Ababa on Monday, according to a police report. The deadly accident occurred in the morning of August 24 when a bucket of the excavator fell on a moving minibus taxi in Bole Subcity of Ethiopia’s capital. Six passengers were killed in the accident, the Addis Ababa Police said in a statement issued Monday. The driver and several other passengers aboard the minibus also sustained serious or minor injuries. They were taken to nearby health facilities for medical treatment, said the Police, who have launched an investigation to determine the exact cause of the accident. The incident is among a series of deadly traffic accidents in the East African nation, which are often linked to reckless driving, weak law enforcement, poor vehicle conditions and other factors. With vehicle numbers rising alongside the country’s growing economy and expanding middle class, experts call for stricter safety enforcement, thorough vehicle inspections, and a more rigorous licensing system to prevent future tragedies. — EM, news agencies

items.title: The overlooked conflict in the Amhara region
items.summary: The last time Aster saw her husband was when he left for work after lunch. As he usually did, he said goodbye to his wife and their two-year-old child before leaving. items.body: The last time Aster saw her husband was when he left for work after lunch. As he usually did, he said goodbye to his wife and their two-year-old child before leaving. It would be the last time Aster saw him alive. Later that day, she called her husband several times. He told her that he and his colleagues were safe but warned her not to leave the house because no one knew what might happen. Aster’s fear stemmed from reports that two federal “army commanders” had been killed on Saturday, 21 October 2023. The area was tense. The two commanders were killed outside a small business run by Aster’s husband. Soldiers accused him of informing Fano fighters about the commanders’ movements, leading to their deaths. The 36-year-old, the owner of the business, and a security guard were taken to a temporary military camp for questioning. Only one of the three returned alive. “I waited until about six in the evening. Then I heard gunshots. I was terrified, but I never thought they would kill him. No one deserves to die like that. It’s not just because he was my husband. He was a kind and generous man who treated everyone the same, whether they were family or strangers. He always put others before himself,” Aster said, her voice breaking with emotion. A few hours after he was taken away, Aster’s husband was found dead on the road. Their child was only two years old at the time. Another man who was killed was a security guard whose body was found near the camp; he had previously served in the defence forces and was a father of three:his wife was eight months pregnant. As the conflict in the Amhara region enters its fourth year, civilians continue to bear the cost of the violence. People like Aster’s husband and the security guard, who were not directly involved in the fighting, have paid the ultimate price. ACLED, which monitors political violence and conflict around the world, said that since the start of the Fano insurgency in April 2023, millions of people in the Amhara region have been affected by violence. Between February and August 2026 alone, more than 8 million people were exposed to conflict. According to ACLED, the violence has affected all parts of the Amhara region, with the heaviest fighting reported in West Gojjam, North Wollo and North Shewa. Both government forces and Fano militias have been accused of committing abuses, although government forces have been blamed for the majority of the reported violations. Observers say the government has not only failed to fulfil its legal and moral responsibility to protect the rights and safety of its citizens, but has also become a perpetrator of abuses. The region has been under a state of emergency since August 2023, with restrictions on civil rights still in place. Reports indicate that many attacks targeting civilians take place after clashes between the two sides, while a significant number of residents have also been killed by heavy weapons that missed their targets and struck civilian areas. Beyond the fighting on the front lines, there have also been targeted killings of government officials. Government forces have also targeted families whose members have joined Fano, with reports of relatives being arrested or killed because of their alleged links to the armed group. The killing of local officials . On 6 June 2024, Milishu Bekele, the administrator of Kewet woreda in North Shewa, was killed on the road. She was six months pregnant at the time and was among the government officials killed by insurgents in the Amhara region. Since the outbreak of the conflict, many local officials have been forced to leave their homes and live inside administrative buildings under tight security, according to their family members. Milishu, who had worked in the health sector for 15 years, was killed while on her way to spend the night at the administrative office. Her husband said she was ambushed by two individuals he identified as Fano members. Officials in Oromia and Tigray have also been killed in attacks linked to their association with the government. ACLED’s 2026 report surveys 66 incidents of violence targeting local officials around the country. The Fano armed group more than doubled its attacks on local officials over the past year, targeting both individuals and public institutions and weakening local administrations. Seen by armed groups as representing opposing interests, local officials have borne a heavy toll from the conflict. The group has targeted woreda administrators, cabinet members and Prosperity Party officials. South Gondar Zone appears to have been particularly affected, with several woreda administrators and government officials killed. One source said local officials who speak out strongly against Fano during meetings are particularly likely to be targeted. The source said the group gathers information on local officials, selects those it wants to target, and sends them threatening messages warning that they will be killed. The source said more than 10 local officials he personally knew had been killed in the zone.The threats against government officials have forced many of them to work remotely or from safer locations.Officials can only travel under strict security arrangements and are often forced to spend the night in military camps for their safety. South Gondar police chief Commander Niggus Tamene said assassinations of local officials increased in 2025 and 2026. Human rights reports indicate that government security forces have subjected the families of Fano members and civilians accused of supporting the group to harassment, threats, arrest, property seizures, killings and other abuses. In August 2024, in Dejen town, six-month-pregnant Nitsuh Mekonen, whose husband had been accused of being a Fano member, was taken from a police station along with her mother-in-law. Both women were later killed, according to relatives. Family members said Nitsuh and five other relatives, including children, had been arrested in an attempt to pressure her husband to return. ACLED data show that fighting between the two sides accounted for about 80% of conflict events recorded in the Amhara region over the past three years, highlighting the scale and spread of the violence. More than eight million people have been exposed to conflict. The conflict in the region tends to intensify during military operations and then subside. ACLED senior analyst Jalale Getachew Birru said these operations can trigger a sharp increase in clashes, often lasting for two weeks or even a month, before the fighting declines. He said the clashes are not confined to battlefields but often take place in villages where people live, making the human toll particularly heavy. An excerpt from a longer report published by BBC Amharic. The post The overlooked conflict in the Amhara region appeared first on Ethiopia Observer .

items.body: Fighting between federal forces and rebels from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which lasted for several hours, ended on Saturday, local and security sources told AFP on Sunday. A TPLF member, speaking on condition of anonymity, said armed clashes in Shererina, near the Sudan border, involving heavy artillery and drone strikes, began at about 6:00 am on Saturday and ended around 5:00 pm. The source said the fighting was slowing down but did not provide any information about casualties. On Saturday, the TPLF accused the federal authorities of escalating their military actions and launching what it described as a “large-scale infantry offensive.” Abraham Belay, head of the Ministry of Irrigation and Lowlands, who is originally from Tigray, confirmed that clashes had erupted between federal forces and TPLF fighters. In a Tigrinya-language statement posted on his official social media page, he accused the TPLF of initiating hostilities in the Shererina area and warned that continued fighting could lead to further harm. The clashes came after tensions between the two sides had intensified in recent months, following that TPLF leaders had dismantled the regional interim administration established by the federal government and taken control. The post Fighting ends between federal forces and TPLF, but calm remains fragile appeared first on Ethiopia Observer .
